fields.title: The Acts of the Apostles
fields.subtitle: Praxeis Apostolōn, “Acts of the Apostles”
fields.description: The second volume of Luke’s two-part work, and the story of how the church began: “you will bear witness to me in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth.” The ascension and the waiting; wind and fire at Pentecost and three thousand baptized; a church devoted to the apostles’ teaching and the prayers; Stephen the first martyr; Philip and the Ethiopian on the desert road; Saul struck down on the Damascus road; Peter at the house of Cornelius, and the council at Jerusalem that opened the door to the Gentiles. Then Paul’s journeys, his speech in Athens, his arrest and trials, the storm and shipwreck, and Rome, where the book ends with the kingdom of God proclaimed “with all boldness, unhindered.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Acts of the Apostles?
qa.answer: The fifth book of the New Testament, the sequel to the Gospel of Luke, and the only history of the first Christians in the Bible. It follows the church from the ascension of Jesus and the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, through the work of Peter in Jerusalem and the spread of the message to Samaria and the Gentiles, to Paul’s journeys and his arrival in Rome as a prisoner, about thirty years later. Its plan is given in Jesus’s words in 1:8.

qa.question: Who wrote Acts, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author, but it is addressed to the same Theophilus as the Gospel of Luke and refers back to that “first book” (1:1). From the second century the church has said both were written by Luke, the doctor who travelled with Paul, and several passages told in the first person (“we”) suggest he was there. Because Acts ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome, around AD 62, some date it soon after; many scholars date it to the 80s.

qa.question: What happened at Pentecost in Acts 2?
qa.answer: Pentecost was the Jewish harvest festival fifty days after Passover. As the disciples were gathered in Jerusalem, a sound like a mighty wind filled the house, tongues like fire rested on each of them, they were filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in other languages, which pilgrims from many nations understood. Peter preached that Jesus, crucified and raised, is Lord and Christ, and about three thousand were baptized. Christians differ on whether the gift of the Spirit with tongues is a pattern for believers today or a once-for-all beginning, but all see it as the birth of the church’s mission.

qa.question: What was the Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15?
qa.answer: A meeting of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, around AD 49, to settle whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved. Peter recalled how God had given the Spirit to the Gentiles at Cornelius’s house, and declared that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. James proposed, and the council agreed, to lay on Gentile believers no burden beyond a few essentials. It was a turning point in the history of the church.

qa.question: Why does Acts end without telling of Paul’s death?
qa.answer: Acts closes with Paul living two years in rented lodgings in Rome, under guard, welcoming everyone and proclaiming the kingdom of God “with all boldness, unhindered” (28:31). Some think Luke wrote before Paul’s trial was decided; others that he ended deliberately with the gospel preached freely at the heart of the empire, its story still unfinished. Early tradition says Paul was put to death in Rome under Nero in the 60s.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
He answered them, “Times and seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority are not yours to know. But when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will bear witness to me in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth.”

— Acts 1:7–8

Acts begins with a backward glance. “Theophilus,” Luke writes, “the first book I composed told of all that Jesus began both to do and to teach.” The word to notice is began. The Gospel told what Jesus began; this second book tells what he went on doing, through his Spirit, in the lives of his followers. It is the only book of its kind in the New Testament, the story of how about a hundred and twenty people gathered in an upper room in Jerusalem became, within a single lifetime, a movement that reached the capital of the world.

Without it we would know almost nothing of how the church began. We would not know of Pentecost, of Stephen, of the Ethiopian on the desert road or the centurion at Caesarea. We would have Paul’s letters, but not the story of his conversion or his journeys, and we would have to guess at the order in which he wrote them. Acts is the bridge between the Gospels and the letters, and it makes sense of both.

The second volume

Acts is the second half of a two-part work by the author of the Gospel of Luke. Both books are addressed to Theophilus; the end of one and the beginning of the other overlap, telling of the risen Jesus’s last words and his being taken up into heaven. Their language, style and concerns are the same: prayer, the Holy Spirit, the poor, the welcome of outsiders, and the steady movement of the story outward from Jerusalem.

From the second century the church has said the author was Luke, a doctor and a companion of Paul. In several passages the narrative slips from “they” into “we”: from Troas to Philippi (16:10–17), on the voyage from Philippi to Jerusalem (20:5–21:18), and on the long, dangerous voyage to Rome (27:1–28:16). Most readers have taken these as the places where the author himself was present. Some scholars think the “we” comes from a source the author used, or is a way of telling a sea story; many others find the simplest explanation the best.

The book ends with Paul in Rome, living for two years under guard in rented lodgings, around AD 60–62. Some think Acts was written soon after, which would explain why it does not tell of Paul’s trial or his death. Many date it later, in the 80s or after. Either way, its author knew the world he wrote about closely. He gets the titles of local officials right, city by city, and his account of the voyage and shipwreck is one of the most detailed descriptions of ancient seafaring that has come down to us. An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio’s time as proconsul of Achaia, before whom Paul was tried in Corinth, to about AD 51, and it has become one of the fixed points from which the dates of Paul’s life are worked out.

Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and the ends of the earth

The risen Jesus gives Acts its table of contents in his last words before he is taken up: they will be his witnesses “in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth.” The book follows that plan:

  • Jerusalem (1–7). The waiting, Pentecost, the first church, the apostles before the council, and the death of Stephen.
  • Judea and Samaria (8–12). The scattering after Stephen’s death, Philip in Samaria and on the desert road, the conversion of Saul, Peter and Cornelius, and the new church at Antioch.
  • To the ends of the earth (13–28). Paul’s journeys through Cyprus, Asia Minor and Greece, the council at Jerusalem, his arrest, his trials before governors and a king, and the voyage to Rome.

Luke marks the stages with short summaries, like milestones: “So God’s word went on spreading”; “the word of God went on growing and spreading”; “with great power the word of the Lord kept growing and gaining strength.” The real hero of Acts is not Peter or Paul. It is the word of God, which cannot be stopped.

Pentecost

For forty days the risen Jesus appears to his apostles and speaks to them about the kingdom of God. Then he is taken up, and they go back to Jerusalem to wait, as he told them, praying together with the women, Mary his mother and his brothers. About ten days later comes the Jewish harvest festival of Pentecost, fifty days after Passover, when Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims from every nation:

When the day of Pentecost had arrived, they were all gathered in one place. All at once a sound came out of heaven, like a mighty wind sweeping through, and it filled the entire house where they sat. Tongues like fire appeared to them, parting so that one came to rest on each of them. Every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in other languages as the Spirit gave them the words to say.

— Acts 2:1–4

The crowd hears these Galileans speaking in their own languages, and Peter stands up to explain. This is what the prophet Joel foretold: God will pour out his Spirit “on all humanity”, sons and daughters, young and old. Jesus, whom they crucified, God has raised from the dead and made “both Lord and Christ”. Pierced to the heart, the crowd asks what they should do. Peter tells them to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of their sins, and they will receive the Holy Spirit as a gift. About three thousand are baptized that day.

Many readers have seen Pentecost as Babel undone. At Babel, in Genesis, human pride was scattered into many languages that could not understand one another. At Pentecost God gathers people of many languages, and each of them hears the mighty deeds of God in his own tongue.

Christians have understood the gift of the Spirit in Acts in different ways. Pentecostal and charismatic believers see in Pentecost and in later scenes in Acts (in Samaria, at Cornelius’s house, at Ephesus) a pattern of a baptism in the Spirit, often with speaking in tongues, that may follow conversion and is meant for every age. Others see Pentecost as a once-for-all beginning, like the giving of the law at Sinai, and the later scenes as marking the gospel’s crossing of new frontiers. All agree that in Acts the Spirit is the one who drives the story.

The first church

Luke pauses to show what the new community was like:

They gave themselves fully to the apostles’ teaching and to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers.

— Acts 2:42

They met in the temple courts and in one another’s homes. They shared what they had, selling land and goods so that no one among them was in need. They ate together “with joyful and simple hearts”. It is an idealised picture, and Luke knows it. A few chapters later he tells of a couple who lied about their gift, and of Greek-speaking widows overlooked in the daily distribution of food, and of the seven men, Stephen among them, appointed to see that it was done fairly. The church in Acts is not perfect. But it is real, and it keeps finding the grace to deal with its failures.

It is also bold. Peter and John, “men without formal schooling”, are arrested after healing a lame man, for teaching that in Jesus there is resurrection from the dead, and ordered to stop speaking of him. Their answer has steadied persecuted believers ever since: “we cannot stay silent about the things we have seen and heard.” When the apostles are arrested again and flogged, they go away glad to have been found worthy to bear shame for the sake of the Name.

Stephen

Stephen is the first martyr. Charged with speaking against the temple and the law, he answers with a long retelling of Israel’s history, showing that God was never confined to one land or one building, and that Israel had often resisted those God sent. His hearers rush at him, drag him out of the city and stone him. As he dies he sees the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand, and he prays as Jesus prayed on the cross:

Then he sank to his knees and cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not charge them with this sin.” With these words he fell asleep.

— Acts 7:60

Luke adds that the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.

The Way opens outward

Stephen’s death sets off a persecution that scatters the believers, and wherever they go they carry the message. Philip preaches in Samaria, to the people Jews had long avoided. Then an angel sends him to a desert road, where an Ethiopian official, a eunuch who has come to Jerusalem to worship, is sitting in his chariot reading Isaiah. “Do you know what it is you are reading?” Philip asks. “How could I,” he answers, “if no one guides me?” Starting from that very passage, Philip tells him the good news about Jesus, and he is baptized by the roadside and travels on with a glad heart.

Then the persecutor himself is stopped. On the road to Damascus, carrying letters to arrest anyone who belongs to “the Way”, Saul is thrown to the ground by a light from heaven and hears a voice: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” Luke thinks this moment so important that he tells it three times: once in the story itself (chapter 9), and twice in Paul’s own words, before a hostile crowd in Jerusalem (22) and before King Agrippa (26). The enemy of the church becomes its greatest missionary, chosen, the Lord says, “to bear my name before Gentiles and kings and the people of Israel.”

The hardest frontier is crossed by Peter. In Caesarea a Roman centurion named Cornelius, a God-fearing Gentile, is told in a vision to send for him; in Joppa, Peter sees a sheet let down from heaven full of animals the law called unclean, and hears a voice telling him not to call unholy what God has made clean. When he arrives at Cornelius’s house and preaches, the Holy Spirit comes down on the Gentile listeners before he has finished speaking. Peter’s words there are a turning point of the book: “In truth I now see that God does not favor one person over another.” Soon afterwards, in Antioch, believers begin to tell the good news to Gentiles as well, and it is there that the disciples are first called Christians.

Paul and the council

From chapter 13 the story belongs mostly to Paul. The church at Antioch, while worshipping and fasting, hears the Spirit say, “Set Barnabas and Saul apart for me”, and sends them out. Acts traces three great journeys, through Cyprus and the cities of southern Asia Minor, then across into Macedonia and Greece, and then a long stay at Ephesus. Paul’s pattern is to go first to the synagogue, where Jews and God-fearing Gentiles gather to hear the Scriptures, and then, when he is driven out, to the Gentiles. Everywhere some believe and others oppose him; he is stoned at Lystra, beaten and jailed at Philippi, and run out of Thessalonica, and everywhere he leaves a church behind.

The success among the Gentiles raised the most important question the early church faced. Must Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved? Some teachers from Judea said they must. Chapter 15 tells how the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem to decide. Peter recalls Cornelius: “we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, and they are saved in just the same way.” James, the brother of Jesus, agrees, and the council writes to the Gentile churches laying on them no burden beyond a few essentials, so that, as many read it, Jewish and Gentile believers could share a table. It is the hinge of Acts and of the whole history of the church. The gospel would not be the property of one nation.

Acts does not hide the church’s disagreements. Paul and Barnabas, partners since the first journey, quarrel so sharply over taking John Mark with them again that they part ways. And later readers have puzzled over how Luke’s account of these years fits Paul’s own in Galatians; scholars still debate which visit to Jerusalem Paul means there.

Athens

One speech in Acts shows how Paul spoke to people who had never read the Scriptures. In Athens, distressed by a city full of idols, he stands before the council of the Areopagus and begins with an altar he has seen, inscribed “To an unknown god.” He tells them of the God who made the world and does not live in temples made by hands, who is not far from any of us. He quotes their own poets: “It is in him that we live and move and exist”, and, “We too are his offspring.” Then he calls them to repent, because God has fixed a day of judgment and has given proof of it by raising a man from the dead. At the mention of the raising of the dead, some scoff. A few believe, among them a member of the council and a woman named Damaris.

The prisoner

The last quarter of Acts tells of Paul’s arrest and trials. He goes up to Jerusalem knowing that chains await him; when friends beg him not to go, he answers that he is ready not only to be bound but to die there “for the name of the Lord Jesus.” In the temple a mob seizes him, and Roman soldiers rescue him. For two years he is held at Caesarea and heard by the governors Felix and Festus and by King Agrippa II. Finally, as a Roman citizen, he appeals to Caesar, and is sent to Rome.

Luke tells the voyage in vivid detail: the late season, the storm, day after day with no sun or stars to be seen, Paul standing on the deck to tell the crew that an angel has promised that not one life will be lost, and the shipwreck on Malta. It is told as an adventure, and it is one. But it is also a picture of what the whole book has shown: no storm, no plot and no prison can stop the word of God from reaching the place God means it to go.

The open ending

Acts does not end with Paul’s trial before Caesar, or with his death, which tradition places in Rome under Nero a few years later. It ends with him in his rented lodgings, welcoming everyone who comes, and the last word in Greek is “unhindered”:

For two full years Paul lived in lodgings he rented, receiving everyone who visited him. There he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught the things about the Lord Jesus Christ, with all boldness, unhindered.

— Acts 28:30–31

Many readers have felt that the ending is open on purpose. The story is not finished, because the witness to the ends of the earth is not finished. Every generation of the church since has been living in the twenty-ninth chapter of Acts.

How to read Acts

Read it first for the story. It is the most exciting book in the New Testament, full of riots, escapes, trials and voyages, and it deserves to be read straight through, perhaps in two or three sittings.

Then read it for its speeches, which make up about a quarter of the book: Peter at Pentecost and in the temple, Stephen before the council, Peter at Cornelius’s house, Paul in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, at Athens, to the elders of Ephesus at Miletus, and in his own defence before the crowd, the governor and the king. Taken together they show how the apostles preached Jesus from the Scriptures to Jews and to Gentiles.

And read it with Paul’s letters beside it. When Acts tells of Philippi or Thessalonica or Corinth or Ephesus, turn to the letters he wrote to those churches, and you will hear the other side of the conversation.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Acts are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Languages.” At Pentecost (2:4) the Greek word for “tongues” is used both for the flames and for what the disciples spoke. This translation says that they spoke in “other languages”, since the crowd heard its own languages. At Caesarea (10:46) and Ephesus (19:6) it keeps the familiar “speaking in tongues”.

“The shared life.” In 2:42 the word often translated “fellowship” is rendered “the shared life”, which says what it was: a life held in common, down to meals and money.

“Brothers and sisters.” Where the Greek word for brothers plainly means the whole community of believers, the translation says “brothers and sisters”.

Verses not found in the oldest manuscripts. Some manuscripts of Acts, chiefly the one called Codex Bezae, have a longer form of the text, with many small additions. This translation follows the shorter text of the earliest manuscripts. So Acts 8:37, in which the Ethiopian confesses his faith before his baptism, is not in the text, nor are 15:34, 24:7 and 28:29, which older Bibles print; the verse numbers are skipped. One more numbering note: in this translation 19:40 includes what most English Bibles number 19:41.

“Christ.” The Open Word Bible lets a reader choose whether Christos reads “Christ” or “the Messiah”. This edition prints “Christ”, but it is worth remembering, in speeches like Peter’s at Pentecost, that the claim being made is that Jesus is Israel’s promised King.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Acts 1
fields.body_html:
Waiting for the promise of the Father

1Theophilus, the first book I composed told of all that Jesus began both to do and to teach, 2until the day he was taken up. Before that, through the Holy Spirit, he had given orders to the apostles he had chosen. 3To them as well he had shown himself alive after he suffered, with many clear proofs, as for forty days he let them see him and told them about the kingdom of God. 4As he shared a meal with them, he charged them not to go away from Jerusalem but to wait there for what the Father had promised: “the promise you heard about from me. 5For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit before many days have passed.”

Jesus is taken up

6When they had gathered, they kept asking him, “Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?” 7He answered them, “Times and seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority are not yours to know. 8But when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will bear witness to me in Jerusalem, through all Judea and Samaria, and out to the farthest end of the earth.” 9With these words said, he was lifted up as they watched, and a cloud received him, so that their eyes could no longer see him. 10As he went, they kept their eyes fixed on the sky, and all at once two men dressed in white were there beside them. 11“Men of Galilee,” they said, “why stand there gazing up at the sky? This Jesus has been taken up from you into heaven, and he will come in the very way you saw him leave for heaven.”

Praying together in the upper room

12Then they went back to Jerusalem from the hill called the Mount of Olives. It lies close to the city, about half a mile away. 13Back in the city, they climbed to the upstairs room where they had been lodging. Peter was there, with John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James. 14All of these were devoted to prayer and of one mind in it. With them were the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.

Matthias joins the apostles

15In those days Peter rose to speak among the brothers and sisters, a crowd of about 120 people gathered in one place. 16“Brothers and sisters, what the Holy Spirit foretold in Scripture by the mouth of David had to come true. He spoke about Judas, who led the way for those who seized Jesus. 17Judas was counted as one of us, and this ministry was given to him as his portion.

18(This man came to own a field, paid for with what he earned by his crime. Falling headfirst, he split open in the middle, and all his bowels gushed out. 19This became common knowledge among all who lived in Jerusalem, and so that piece of land came to be known in their own language as Hakeldama, which means Field of Blood.) 20For it is written in the book of Psalms, ‘May his home become a ruin, with no one living in it,’ and, ‘Let someone else take over his post.’ 21So we need one of the men who kept company with us all through the time the Lord Jesus came and went among us, 22from the day John baptized up to the day he was taken from us. One of these must join us as a witness to his resurrection.” 23They proposed two men, Joseph who was called Barsabbas and was also known as Justus, and Matthias. 24And they prayed, “Lord, you who know the hearts of all people, make plain which one of these two is your choice 25to fill the place in this ministry and apostleship that Judas deserted to go to his own place.” 26They drew lots for the two, the lot fell on Matthias, and from then on he was counted with the eleven apostles.
fields.summary: The risen Jesus tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Father, the Holy Spirit, and is taken up into heaven. The believers pray together, and Matthias is chosen to take the place of Judas.

fields.title: Acts 2
fields.body_html:
The day of Pentecost

1When the day of Pentecost had arrived, they were all gathered in one place. 2All at once a sound came out of heaven, like a mighty wind sweeping through, and it filled the entire house where they sat. 3Tongues like fire appeared to them, parting so that one came to rest on each of them. 4Every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in other languages as the Spirit gave them the words to say.

5Devout Jews from every nation in the world were living in Jerusalem. 6At this sound the people flocked together, and they were bewildered, for each one heard them speaking in their own language. 7Astonished and full of wonder, they said, “Surely all these people speaking are from Galilee, are they not? 8So how is it that each of us hears them in the language we grew up speaking? 9We are Parthians, Medes and Elamites; we live in Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, 10Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; some of us are visitors from Rome, 11Jews and converts to Judaism; we are Cretans and Arabs. Yet we hear them telling in our own languages the mighty deeds of God!” 12Everyone was astonished and at a loss, and they kept saying to one another, “What can this be?” 13But some jeered at them: “They have drunk too much sweet wine!”

Peter speaks to the crowd

14Then Peter stood up with the Eleven, lifted his voice, and spoke out to them: “Jewish people, and everyone living in Jerusalem, know this, and pay close attention to my words. 15They are not drunk, as you imagine. The day is only three hours old; it is nine in the morning. 16No, this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: 17‘In the last days it will happen, God says, that I will pour out my Spirit on all humanity. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy; your young men will see visions, and your old men will have dreams. 18In those days I will pour out my Spirit even on my servants, men and women alike, and they will prophesy. 19I will work wonders up in the sky and signs down on the earth: blood and fire and a haze of smoke. 20The sun will turn dark and the moon to blood before the great and splendid day of the Lord arrives. 21Then whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’

Jesus, raised and exalted

22People of Israel, listen to what I am saying: Jesus of Nazareth was a man whom God commended to you by deeds of power, wonders and signs that God worked through him among you, as you well know. 23God had set the plan and known it beforehand: he was handed over, and you, through the hands of lawless men, fastened him to a cross and killed him. 24But God raised him up and freed him from the pains of death, since there was no way death could hold him fast. 25David says of him: ‘I kept the Lord always in view before me; with him at my right hand I will not be moved. 26So my heart is full of gladness and my tongue sings for joy; even my body will settle down in hope, 27for you will not abandon me to the world of the dead or allow your Holy One to experience decay. 28You have taught me the roads that lead to life, and being with you will fill me with gladness.’

29Brothers and sisters, I may speak to you plainly about our ancestor David: he died and was buried, and his tomb is here with us to this very day. 30But he was a prophet, and he knew that God had sworn an oath to him to seat one of his own descendants on his throne. 31So he looked ahead and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ: he was not abandoned to the world of the dead, and his body never saw decay. 32It is this Jesus whom God raised up, and every one of us is a witness to it. 33So now he has been lifted up to the right hand of God. From the Father he received the promised Holy Spirit, and he has poured it out. This is what you are seeing and hearing. 34David himself never went up into heaven, but he says, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: “Take your seat at my right hand 35until I set your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet.”‘ 36So let the whole house of Israel know for certain: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.”

What shall we do?

37These words pierced their hearts. They asked Peter and the rest of the apostles, “What are we to do, brothers?” 38Peter answered them, “Repent, and every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, so that your sins may be forgiven; and you will receive the Holy Spirit as a gift. 39The promise belongs to you and your children, and to all who are far away, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.” 40He went on to bear witness with many more words and kept appealing to them: “Let yourselves be rescued from this crooked generation!” 41Then those who welcomed what he said were baptized; that day about 3,000 people joined them. 42They gave themselves fully to the apostles’ teaching and to the shared life, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers.

The believers share their lives

43Everyone felt a deep awe, and many wonders and signs took place through the apostles. 44Everyone who believed kept together and treated all they had as shared. 45They would sell off land and goods and divide the money among all, according to what each one needed. 46Day after day they went on gathering, united, in the temple; at home they broke bread, eating their food with joyful and simple hearts, 47praising God and well regarded by all the people. And each day the Lord brought into their company more people who were being saved.
fields.summary: On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit comes on the believers, and they speak in other languages. Peter tells the crowd that God raised Jesus and made Jesus Lord, about three thousand are baptized, and the believers share their lives and possessions.

fields.title: Acts 3
fields.body_html:
A man lame from birth walks

1Peter and John were on their way up to the temple for the afternoon prayer at three o’clock. 2Some people were carrying there a man who had been lame since birth. Every day they set him down by the temple gate known as the Beautiful Gate, so that he could beg from the people going in. 3When he saw Peter and John about to enter the temple, he begged them for a gift. 4Peter, together with John, gazed straight at him and said, “Look at us.” 5He kept his eyes on them, hoping they would give him something. 6But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but I will give you what I do have. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk!” 7Peter took him by the right hand and lifted him up. At once the man’s feet and ankles grew firm; 8he sprang up, stood, and walked about. He went with them into the temple, walking and leaping and praising God. 9Everyone there saw him walking about and praising God. 10They knew him as the man who used to sit begging at the temple’s Beautiful Gate, and they were filled with awe and astonishment at what had happened to him.

Peter speaks in Solomon’s Porch

11As he clung to Peter and John, the whole crowd came running to them in what was called Solomon’s Porch, completely astonished. 12When Peter saw this, he addressed the people: “People of Israel, why are you amazed at this? Why fix your eyes on us, as if it were our own power or piety that made this man walk? 13The God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob, the God of our ancestors, has glorified his servant Jesus. You handed him over and rejected him before Pilate, even when Pilate had judged that he should be set free. 14You turned your backs on the Holy and Righteous One and asked to have a murderer granted to you as a favor, 15and you killed the Author of life. God raised him from the dead; we are witnesses to that. 16This man you see and know was made strong by the name of Jesus, through faith in that name. The faith that comes through him has given the man perfect health here in front of you all.

Repent and turn back

17Now, brothers and sisters, I know you did not understand what you were doing, and neither did your rulers. 18Yet by these events God made come true what he had said beforehand through all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer. 19Repent, then, and turn around, so that your sins may be erased, 20that seasons of relief may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send you Jesus, the Christ he appointed for you beforehand. 21Jesus must be welcomed into heaven and remain there until the time when everything is set right again, as God told long ago by the mouth of his holy prophets. 22Moses himself said, ‘From among your own people the Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you, one like me. Whatever he says to you, you must heed him in all of it. 23Every person who refuses to heed that prophet will be destroyed and removed from the people.’ 24And every prophet who has spoken, from Samuel on through those who followed him, has also told of these days. 25You are the children of the prophets and of the covenant God made with your ancestors when he said to Abraham, ‘All the families of the earth will be blessed through your offspring.’ 26It was for you first that God raised up his servant and sent him to bless you, turning each one of you away from your evil deeds.”
fields.summary: Peter and John heal a man lame from birth at the temple gate. In Solomon’s Porch Peter tells the astonished crowd that this was done in the name of Jesus, whom God raised, and calls them to repent and turn back.

fields.title: Acts 4
fields.body_html:
Peter and John taken into custody

1Peter and John were still speaking to the people when the priests, the commander of the temple guard and the Sadducees confronted them. 2These men were deeply irritated that the apostles were teaching the people and declaring that in Jesus there is resurrection from the dead. 3They took hold of them and, because evening had already come, kept them under guard until the next day. 4Even so, many who heard the message came to believe, and the count of men rose to about 5,000.

No other name under heaven

5The next day the people’s rulers, elders and experts in the law met together in Jerusalem. 6Annas the high priest was there, with Caiaphas, John, Alexander and all the others from the high priest’s family. 7They had the two men stand in the center of the gathering and began questioning them: “What sort of power, or what sort of name, did you use to do this?” 8Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Leaders of the people and elders, 9since we are being questioned today about a kindness done for a disabled man, and how he was made well, 10then all of you, and the whole people of Israel, must understand this. It was done in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead. Through him this man is standing in front of you, sound and whole. 11He is the stone that you builders scorned as worthless, and he has become the head of the corner. 12Salvation comes through no one but him. Under all of heaven God has given humankind no other name through which we are to be saved.”

We cannot stop speaking

13The council members saw how freely Peter and John spoke, and they realized these were men without formal schooling, just ordinary people. This astonished them, and they recognized that the two had been companions of Jesus. 14But with the healed man standing right there beside them, they could say nothing to refute it. 15So they ordered them to step out of the council room, and then they talked the matter over among themselves. 16They said, “What can we do with these men? A remarkable sign has clearly been done through them; the whole population of Jerusalem can see it, and there is no way we can say it did not happen. 17Still, this must not spread more widely among the people. Let us threaten them, so that they never again speak to anyone in this name.” 18They called the two men back and gave them a strict order: they were not to speak or teach in the name of Jesus in any way at all. 19But Peter and John answered them, “You must decide whether, in God’s sight, it is right to heed you rather than God. 20For our part, we cannot stay silent about the things we have seen and heard.” 21The council threatened them still more and then set them free. They could see no way to punish them because of the people, who were all giving glory to God for what had happened. 22This sign of healing had happened to a man more than forty years old.

The believers pray for boldness

23As soon as they were set free, the two went back to their fellow believers and gave an account of everything the chief priests and elders had told them. 24When they heard it, they lifted their voices to God together and prayed: “Sovereign Master, maker of heaven and earth, of the sea, and of everything they hold! 25It was you who spoke by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of our father David, your servant: ‘Why were the nations in an uproar, and why did the peoples scheme for nothing? 26The kings of the earth took up their positions, and the rulers joined forces against the Lord and against his Christ.’ 27In truth, here in this very city, Herod and Pontius Pilate assembled with the nations and with the peoples of Israel against your holy servant Jesus, the one you anointed. 28They carried out everything that your power and your purpose had already settled must take place. 29Now, Lord, take notice of their threats. Let your slaves speak your word with complete boldness, 30while you put out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are done through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” 31When they finished praying, the place where they had met shook, and every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they went on proclaiming God’s word fearlessly.

One heart and soul

32The whole company of believers shared a single heart and soul. Not one of them treated anything they owned as theirs alone; everything they had belonged to them all. 33With mighty power the apostles went on declaring that the Lord Jesus had risen, and God’s grace rested richly on them all. 34No one among them lacked anything, since any who owned fields or houses would sell them and bring what the sale had raised. 35They laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was shared out to each person as each one had need. 36One of them was Joseph, a Levite born in Cyprus, to whom the apostles gave the name Barnabas, meaning “one who encourages.” 37He sold a field that he owned, then brought the money and set it down at the apostles’ feet.
fields.summary: Peter and John are taken into custody and tell the council that there is salvation in no other name under heaven. Released, they and the believers pray for boldness, and the believers share everything with one heart and soul.

fields.title: Acts 5
fields.body_html:
The lie of Ananias and Sapphira

1A man called Ananias, however, sold a piece of land together with his wife Sapphira. 2He secretly set aside some of the proceeds, and his wife knew of it. Then he brought the remaining portion and laid it at the apostles’ feet. 3Peter said, “Ananias, why did Satan fill your heart, to make you lie to the Holy Spirit and keep part of the land’s price back? 4Before it was sold, was it not your own? And after the sale, was the money not yours to use as you chose? Why did you set your heart on doing this? It is not human beings you have lied to, but God.” 5As Ananias heard these words he fell down and died, and a great fear came over everyone who heard about it. 6The young men stood up, wound him in a cloth, carried him out and buried him.

7Some three hours later his wife arrived, unaware of what had taken place. 8Peter said to her, “Tell me, did the two of you sell the land for this amount?” “Yes,” she replied, “that was the price.” 9Peter said to her, “Why did the two of you agree together to put the Spirit of the Lord to the test? Look, the men who buried your husband are already at the door. They will carry you out as well.” 10Instantly she collapsed at Peter’s feet and died. The young men came in, found her dead, and carried her out to bury her next to her husband. 11The entire church was filled with deep fear, as was everyone who heard about these things.

Signs and wonders among the people

12By the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders kept taking place among the people. With one mind, the believers all gathered in Solomon’s Porch. 13None of the others dared to associate with them, yet the people thought highly of them. 14Still more believers were brought to the Lord, great numbers of men and women alike. 15People would even carry their sick out into the streets and lay them on cots and pallets, hoping that when Peter came along, his shadow, if nothing more, might fall across some of them. 16People streamed in, too, from the towns near Jerusalem. They brought those who were sick or harassed by unclean spirits, and every one of them was made well.

An angel opens the prison doors

17But the high priest rose to act, and with him all who sided with him, the Sadducee party. Burning with jealousy, 18they took hold of the apostles and shut them up in the public prison. 19That night, though, an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the prison. He led them outside and said to them, 20“Go and take your stand in the temple, and tell the people the whole message of this life.” 21Hearing this, they went into the temple at first light and began to teach.

Meanwhile the high priest and his party arrived. They summoned the council together with all the elders of Israel, and sent orders to the prison to bring the apostles. 22The officers went, but they did not find the apostles in the prison. They came back with this report: 23“The prison was shut and fully secured when we got there, and the guards were at their posts by the doors. But once we had opened up, we found nobody inside.” 24The report left the captain of the temple and the chief priests puzzled about the apostles, unsure what all this would come to. 25Then a man arrived with news for them: “Those men you locked up are in the temple right now, standing there teaching the people!” 26The captain then went with his officers and fetched the apostles. They used no violence, for they were afraid of the crowd and of being stoned.

Obeying God rather than people

27They brought them in and stood them before the council. The high priest began to question them: 28“We ordered you in no uncertain terms to stop teaching in this name. Now look: your teaching has spread all through Jerusalem, and you are set on laying this man’s blood at our door.” 29Peter and the other apostles replied, “It is God we must obey rather than people. 30The God of our ancestors raised Jesus, whom you had done away with by hanging him on a tree. 31He is the one God has lifted up to his right hand as Leader and Savior, to grant Israel repentance and forgiveness of sins. 32We ourselves testify to these things, and so does the Holy Spirit, given by God to all who obey him.”

Gamaliel’s counsel

33Hearing this, the council members were enraged and were ready to have the apostles killed. 34But one of the council stood up, a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law respected by the whole people. He had the men sent outside for a short time, 35and then he spoke to the council: “Men of Israel, be careful how you deal with these men. 36In days gone by Theudas came forward, making himself out to be someone great, and around 400 men took his side. He was killed, those who had followed his lead were broken up, and nothing was left of it. 37After him came Judas the Galilean, at the time of the census, who drew a following of people after him. He also perished, and those who had followed his lead were all scattered abroad. 38So here is what I say to you now: keep clear of these men and let them be. If this plan or this work has a human source, it will fall apart, 39but if it comes from God, you will not be able to bring them down. You may even turn out to be at war with God.” Gamaliel’s words won them over. 40They summoned the apostles, had them beaten, and commanded them to stop speaking in the name of Jesus. Then they released them. 41As they went out from the council, the apostles were glad: they had been found worthy to bear shame for the sake of the Name. 42Every day, both in the temple and in people’s homes, they went on teaching without a break, and announcing the good news that the Christ is Jesus.
fields.summary: Ananias and Sapphira lie about their gift and fall dead. The apostles do many signs, an angel opens the prison doors, and before the council they answer that they must obey God rather than people; Gamaliel advises the council to leave them alone.

fields.title: Acts 6
fields.body_html:
Seven chosen to serve the widows

1In those days, while the number of disciples kept growing, the Greek-speaking believers began to grumble against those who spoke Hebrew. Their widows, they said, were being passed over when food was given out each day. 2So the Twelve called the whole company of the disciples together and said, “It is not fitting for us to leave aside the word of God in order to serve at tables. 3So, brothers and sisters, look among yourselves for seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, and we will put them in charge of this need. 4As for us, we will hold fast to prayer and to the service of the word.” 5The whole gathering approved of what was said. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, together with Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a convert to Judaism from Antioch. 6They had these men stand before the apostles, and after praying, they laid their hands on them.

The word grows, and Stephen is seized

7So God’s word went on spreading. In Jerusalem the disciples grew greatly in number, and large numbers of priests were coming to obey the faith. 8Stephen was full of grace and power, and he worked wonders and great signs among the people. 9Then opposition rose up from the synagogue known as the Freedmen’s, with Cyrenians and Alexandrians and people from Cilicia and Asia, and they began debating with Stephen. 10Yet the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke were too much for them; they could not hold their ground. 11Then they quietly got some men to say, “We have heard this man utter blasphemies against Moses and against God.” 12They roused the people, the elders and the scribes. They came upon Stephen, seized him, and took him before the council. 13There they put up false witnesses, who said, “This man keeps on talking against the holy place and against the law. 14We heard him say that this Jesus, the Nazarene, will pull this place down and alter the customs Moses passed on to us.” 15Everyone seated in the council fixed their eyes on Stephen, and they saw that his face looked like an angel’s.
fields.summary: Seven men, Stephen among them, are chosen to serve the widows so the apostles can give themselves to prayer and the word. The word grows, and Stephen is seized and brought before the council on false charges.

fields.title: Acts 7
fields.body_html:
Stephen answers the council

1The high priest asked, “Are these charges true?” 2Stephen replied, “Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran. 3God said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kin, and come to the land that I will show you.’ 4So he left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. After his father’s death, God moved him from there into this land where you now live. 5He gave him no share of it to inherit, not even ground enough for one step. But he promised to give it to him and to his descendants after him to hold as their own, while Abraham was still childless. 6This is what God said: his descendants would live as outsiders in a land that belonged to others, and its people would make them slaves and treat them harshly for 400 years. 7‘But I will judge the nation they serve as slaves,’ God said, ‘and afterward they will come out and worship me in this place.’ 8God also gave him the covenant marked by circumcision. And so, when Isaac was born to Abraham, he circumcised him on the eighth day. Isaac in turn had Jacob, and Jacob had the twelve patriarchs.

9The patriarchs envied Joseph and sold him off to Egypt. Yet God stood by him 10and delivered him from every hardship he met. He gave him favor and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him governor over Egypt and over all his household. 11Then famine struck the whole of Egypt and Canaan, bringing great hardship, and our ancestors could find nothing to eat. 12When Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt, he sent our forefathers there on a first journey. 13On their second visit Joseph let his brothers know who he was, and Pharaoh learned about Joseph’s family. 14Joseph sent for his father Jacob and for all his relatives, seventy-five people in all, 15and Jacob went down to Egypt. There he died, and so did our forefathers. 16They were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor at Shechem.

The people grow in Egypt, and Moses is born

17The time was coming close for the promise God had pledged to Abraham, and the people grew and multiplied in Egypt 18until another king rose to rule Egypt, a king who knew nothing of Joseph. 19He schemed against our people and treated our ancestors cruelly. He made them put their babies out to die. 20That was the time when Moses was born, and he was a beautiful child before God. For three months he was cared for in his father’s house. 21When he was put outside, Pharaoh’s daughter took him in and raised him as her own son. 22Moses was schooled in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he had power in what he said and in what he did.

23As he reached the age of forty, he set his heart on visiting his own kin, the people of Israel. 24Seeing one of them being wronged, he stepped in to defend him. He struck down the Egyptian and so avenged the man who was being abused. 25He supposed his kin would grasp that God was bringing them salvation through his hand, but they did not grasp it. 26On the following day he came upon some of them as they fought, and he tried to bring them back to peace: ‘Men, you are brothers. Why are you wronging each other?’ 27But the one who was abusing his neighbor thrust Moses away and said, ‘Who put you in charge as ruler and judge over us? 28Do you mean to kill me the way you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ 29At these words Moses fled, and he lived as a foreigner in the land of Midian, where he had two sons.

The voice from the burning bush

30When forty more years had gone by, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire within a bush. 31Moses was amazed when he saw this sight. As he went closer to look, the voice of the Lord came to him: 32‘I am the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.’ Moses was seized with trembling and did not dare to look. 33The Lord said to him, ‘Take the sandals off your feet, because the place where you are standing is holy ground. 34I have seen, yes, seen the cruelty done to my people in Egypt. I have heard them groaning, and I have come down to rescue them. Come now: I will send you to Egypt.’

35This was the Moses they had pushed away with the words ‘Who made you ruler and judge?’ God sent this very man to be both ruler and redeemer, with the help of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. 36It was he who brought them out, working wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years. 37This is the Moses who told the people of Israel, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your own people.’ 38He was there in the assembly in the wilderness, with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai and with our ancestors, and he received living words to pass on to us. 39Yet our ancestors would not submit to him. They thrust him aside, and their hearts went back to Egypt. 40‘Make us gods to lead the way for us,’ they told Aaron. ‘This Moses who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we have no idea what has become of him.’ 41Then it was that they fashioned a calf. They offered a sacrifice to the idol and held a celebration over the work of their hands. 42So God turned away and gave them over to worship the stars of the sky, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring me slaughtered animals and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel? 43You lifted up the tent of Moloch and the star of the god Rephan, the images you made in order to bow down to them. So I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’

The tent in the wilderness and the house Solomon built

44In the wilderness our ancestors had the tent of the testimony, made as he who spoke to Moses had directed, following the pattern Moses had seen. 45Our ancestors received it in their turn and brought it in with Joshua when they took possession of the lands of the nations, whom God drove out ahead of them. So it was until the days of David. 46God looked on David with favor, and David asked to be allowed to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. 47But it was Solomon who built a house for him. 48Yet the Most High does not make his home in buildings that hands have made, as the prophet says: 49‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool under my feet. What sort of house could you build for me, says the Lord, or what place could be my resting place? 50Was it not my hand that made all these things?’ 51How stubborn you are! Your hearts and ears are uncircumcised. You are forever fighting against the Holy Spirit, and you do what your ancestors did. 52Which one of the prophets escaped persecution by your ancestors? They killed those who told in advance of the coming of the Righteous One, and you have now become his betrayers and murderers. 53The law was given to you through angels, but you have not kept it.”

Stephen sees the Son of Man, and is stoned

54Hearing these words, they seethed with fury and ground their teeth at Stephen. 55Filled with the Holy Spirit, Stephen fixed his gaze on heaven. He saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. 56He said, “Look! I see the heavens opened wide, and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand.” 57They let out a great shout, covered their ears, and rushed at him all together. 58They drove him out of the city and began to stone him. The witnesses put their cloaks down at the feet of a young man named Saul. 59As they stoned Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” 60Then he sank to his knees and cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not charge them with this sin.” With these words he fell asleep.
fields.summary: Stephen answers the council with the story of Israel from Abraham through Joseph, Moses and the tent in the wilderness to the house Solomon built, and accuses them of resisting the Holy Spirit. Stephen sees the Son of Man at God’s right hand and is stoned, with Saul looking on.

fields.title: Acts 8
fields.body_html:
The church scattered

1Saul, for his part, gave his full approval to Stephen’s death.

That same day a fierce persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and everyone except the apostles was driven out into the country districts of Judea and Samaria. 2Some devout men gave Stephen a burial and mourned loudly for him. 3Saul, however, set about destroying the church. He went from house to house, hauled off men and women alike, and had them put in prison.

Philip in Samaria

4Those who had been scattered went from place to place, announcing the good news of the message. 5Philip went down to the city of Samaria and began to proclaim the Christ to the people there. 6The crowds, one and all, listened closely to what Philip said, as they heard him and saw the signs he performed. 7Unclean spirits came out of many people, shrieking as they left, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. 8So there was great joy in that city.

Simon, who practiced magic

9Now there was a man named Simon who had been in the city for some time, working magic and astonishing the people of Samaria. He made himself out to be someone great, 10and everyone, from the least to the most important, hung on his words. “This man,” they said, “is the power of God that is called Great.” 11They followed him because for a long while he had dazzled them with his magic. 12But when Philip announced the good news of God’s kingdom and of the name of Jesus Christ, they believed him, and both men and women were baptized. 13Even Simon himself believed, and after he was baptized he stayed close to Philip. When he saw the signs and great miracles that were happening, he was astounded.

14When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. 15The two went down and prayed for the people there to receive the Holy Spirit, 16for the Spirit had not yet come down on any of them. They had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. 17Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. 18Simon saw that the Spirit was given when the apostles laid their hands on people, and he offered them money. 19“Let me have this power too,” he said, “so that whoever I place my hands on will receive the Holy Spirit.” 20Peter answered him, “To ruin with you and your silver! You thought you could get the gift of God with money. 21You have no part or portion in this, because in God’s eyes your heart is not right. 22So turn from this wickedness of yours and pray to the Lord. It may be that he will forgive you for what you had in your heart, 23For I can see that you are full of bitter poison and bound by wrongdoing.” 24Simon replied, “Pray to the Lord for me yourselves, so that none of the things you have said will happen to me.”

25After Peter and John had borne witness and spoken the word of the Lord, they set out back to Jerusalem, announcing the good news in many Samaritan villages on the way.

Philip and the Ethiopian official

26An angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Get ready and head south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” (This is a desert road.) 27So Philip got up and went. And there on the road was a man from Ethiopia, a eunuch, a high official in charge of all the treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. He had come to Jerusalem to worship, 28and now he was on his way home, seated in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah. 29The Spirit told Philip, “Go up to that chariot and stay with it.” 30Philip ran over to him and heard him reading aloud from the prophet Isaiah. “Do you know what it is you are reading?” he asked. 31“How could I,” he said, “if no one guides me?” He asked Philip to climb up and sit beside him. 32The passage of Scripture he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led away to be slaughtered, and like a lamb that makes no sound while it is sheared, he did not open his mouth. 33When he was humiliated, justice was denied him. Who can speak of his descendants? For his life is taken away from the earth.” 34The eunuch said to Philip, “Please tell me, who is the prophet talking about here? Is he speaking of himself, or of another person?” 35Then Philip spoke up. Starting from that very Scripture, he made Jesus known to him as good news. 36As they traveled on along the road, they came to some water. “There is water here!” the eunuch exclaimed. “Is there any reason I should not be baptized?” 38He gave orders to halt the chariot, and the two of them, Philip and the eunuch, went down into the water, and Philip baptized him. 39When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away. The eunuch did not see him again, but he traveled on with a glad heart. 40Philip, for his part, turned up at Azotus. He went on through the region, announcing the good news in every town until he reached Caesarea.
fields.summary: After Stephen’s death the church is scattered, and Saul tries to destroy it. Philip proclaims the good news in Samaria, where Simon who practiced magic is rebuked, and on the desert road Philip baptizes an Ethiopian official.

fields.title: Acts 9
fields.body_html:
Saul on the road to Damascus

1Saul, however, still breathed threats and murder against the Lord’s disciples. Going to the high priest, 2he requested letters to the synagogues of Damascus. With them he could put in chains any people of the Way he found there, men and women alike, and take them back to Jerusalem. 3On his way, as he was nearing Damascus, all at once a light from heaven blazed around him. 4He dropped to the ground and heard a voice speaking to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” 5“Who are you, Lord?” he asked. He answered, “I am Jesus, and you are persecuting me. 6But get up and go into the city. There you will be told what you have to do.” 7The men on the road with him stood there unable to speak. They heard the voice, but they saw no one. 8Saul rose from the ground. His eyes were open, yet he saw nothing at all, and his companions had to lead him by the hand into Damascus. 9He was without sight for three days, and all that time he neither ate nor drank.

The Lord sends Ananias to Saul

10Living in Damascus was a disciple by the name of Ananias. In a vision the Lord called him: “Ananias!” “I am here, Lord,” he answered. 11The Lord said to him, “Get up and go to the street called Straight. There, at the house of Judas, look for a man of Tarsus by the name of Saul. Even now he is praying, 12and he has seen a vision in which a man named Ananias comes in and lays his hands on him so that he can see again.” 13But Ananias answered, “Lord, many have told me of this man, and of how much evil he did to your holy people in Jerusalem. 14Now he is here, and the chief priests have given him power to put in chains all who call on your name.” 15But the Lord told him, “Go, because I have chosen this man as a vessel to bear my name before Gentiles and kings and the people of Israel. 16I myself will show him how much he will have to suffer for the sake of my name.” 17So Ananias went off and entered the house. He put his hands on Saul and said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road you traveled, has sent me so that your sight may come back and you may be filled with the Holy Spirit.” 18All at once what looked like scales fell away from his eyes, and he could see. He stood up and was baptized; 19then he took food and grew strong again.

Saul proclaims Jesus in Damascus and Jerusalem

Saul stayed for some days with the disciples in Damascus. 20Without delay he went into the synagogues and proclaimed Jesus, telling them that he is the Son of God. 21All who heard him were astonished. “Is this not the man who tried to destroy those in Jerusalem who call on this name?” they said. “Did he not come here for this very purpose, to take them in chains to the chief priests?” 22But Saul’s power kept growing. He threw the Jews who lived in Damascus into confusion, demonstrating that Jesus is the Christ.

23After a good many days, the Jews made a plan to kill him. 24But Saul learned of their plot. They were even guarding the gates around the clock, waiting for the chance to kill him. 25One night, though, his disciples took him and got him out through the wall, letting him down in a basket.

26Once in Jerusalem, Saul made attempts to join the disciples, but every one of them feared him; they could not believe that he had become a disciple. 27Barnabas, however, took him in hand and brought him to the apostles. He explained to them that on the road Saul had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him, and that in Damascus Saul had spoken out without fear in the name of Jesus. 28From then on Saul was with them, going in and out among them in Jerusalem and speaking openly in the name of the Lord. 29He spoke with the Greek-speaking Jews and argued with them, but they began making attempts on his life. 30When the brothers and sisters came to know of it, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him on his way to Tarsus.

31So it was that the church across all of Judea, Galilee and Samaria had peace. It was being built up and walked in the fear of the Lord, and with the Holy Spirit’s encouragement its numbers kept growing.

Aeneas is healed at Lydda

32Peter was traveling about through the whole area, and he came down to visit the holy people living in Lydda. 33There he came upon a man called Aeneas, a paralyzed man who had been confined to his bed for eight years. 34Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ is healing you. Get up and make your bed.” He got up at once. 35Everyone living in Lydda and the plain of Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.

Tabitha is raised at Joppa

36At Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha; translated, the name is Dorcas, which means gazelle. Her days were full of good works and of the gifts she gave to the poor. 37Just at that time she fell ill and died. They washed her body and laid it in an upper room. 38Lydda was not far from Joppa, and when the disciples heard that Peter was there, they sent two men to him with the plea, “Please come to us without delay.” 39Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him up to the upper room. All the widows stood around him in tears, holding up the tunics and cloaks Dorcas would make when she was among them. 40Peter made everyone leave the room. He knelt and prayed, then turned to the body and said, “Tabitha, stand up.” She opened her eyes, and at the sight of Peter she sat up. 41Peter gave her his hand and raised her up. Then he called in the holy people and the widows and presented her to them, alive. 42Word of this went all through Joppa, and many came to believe in the Lord. 43Peter stayed on in Joppa for many days, as the guest of one Simon, a tanner.
fields.summary: On the road to Damascus the risen Lord confronts Saul, who is blinded and then healed and baptized by Ananias. Saul proclaims Jesus in Damascus and Jerusalem, and Peter heals Aeneas at Lydda and raises Tabitha at Joppa.

fields.title: Acts 10
fields.body_html:
An angel comes to Cornelius

1In Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion in what was called the Italian Cohort. 2He was a devout man who feared God, as did his whole household. He gave generously to the poor among the Jewish people and prayed to God at all times. 3One afternoon at about three o’clock he had a vision. He saw plainly an angel of God come in to him and say, “Cornelius!” 4Cornelius stared at him in fear and said, “What is it, sir?” The angel answered, “Your prayers and your gifts to the poor have risen before God, and he has remembered you. 5Now send some men to Joppa and have them bring back a man named Simon, the one called Peter. 6He is a guest of another Simon, a tanner, whose house stands by the sea.” 7As soon as the angel who had spoken to him was gone, Cornelius called two of his household servants and one of the soldiers who attended him, a devout man. 8He told them all that had happened and sent them off to Joppa.

What God has made clean

9The next day, while the men were still on the road and nearing the town, Peter went up on the roof to pray. It was about noon. 10He grew hungry and wanted something to eat. While the food was being prepared, he fell into a trance. 11He saw heaven standing open and something like a large sheet coming down, lowered to the ground by its four corners. 12In it were all kinds of four-footed animals, creatures that crawl on the ground, and birds of the air. 13Then a voice said to him, “Get up, Peter. Slaughter and eat.” 14“Certainly not, Lord!” Peter replied. “Nothing unholy or unclean has ever passed my lips.” 15The voice spoke to him a second time: “What God has made clean, you must not call unholy.” 16This happened three times, and then at once the sheet was taken back up into heaven.

17Peter was still wondering what to make of the vision he had seen when the men sent by Cornelius, who had found their way to Simon’s house, arrived at the gate. 18They called out, asking whether Simon known as Peter was a guest there. 19While Peter was still turning the vision over in his mind, the Spirit said to him, “Some men are here looking for you. 20Get up, go downstairs, and go with them without any hesitation, because I have sent them.” 21So Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the man you are looking for. Why have you come?” 22They replied, “We come from Cornelius the centurion, an upright man who fears God and is respected by all the Jewish people. A holy angel instructed him to send for you to come to his house, so that he could hear what you have to say.” 23Peter invited them in and had them stay as his guests.

Peter goes to a Gentile’s house

The next day he set out with them, and some of the believers from Joppa came along with him. 24The day after that, he arrived in Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them and had gathered his relatives and close friends. 25As Peter came in, Cornelius met him, fell at his feet, and bowed down before him. 26But Peter pulled him to his feet. “Stand up,” he said. “I am only a human being myself.” 27Still talking with him, Peter went inside and found a large gathering of people. 28He said to them, “You know well that it is not permitted for a Jew to keep company with a foreigner or to enter a foreigner’s home. But God has shown me that I must not call anyone unholy or unclean. 29That is why I came without raising any objection when you sent for me. So may I ask why you sent for me?”

30Cornelius answered, “Four days ago, at this very hour, three in the afternoon, I was in my house praying. Suddenly a man in shining clothes stood in front of me. 31He said, ‘Cornelius, God has heard your prayer and has remembered your gifts to the poor. 32So send to Joppa and ask Simon, who is called Peter, to come. He is staying as a guest in the home of Simon the tanner, by the sea.’ 33I sent for you right away, and it was good of you to come. Now we are all here before God, ready to listen to everything the Lord has instructed you to say.”

God does not favor one person over another

34Then Peter began to speak: “In truth I now see that God does not favor one person over another. 35Instead, in every nation he accepts those who fear him and practice righteousness. 36This is the message he sent to the people of Israel, bringing the good news that peace has come through Jesus Christ, and Jesus is Lord of all. 37You yourselves know the events that took place across all Judea. They began in Galilee, after the baptism John proclaimed. 38They concern Jesus from Nazareth: God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, and he traveled from place to place doing good and healing everyone the devil held in his grip, because God was with him. 39We ourselves saw all that he did, both in the Jewish countryside and in Jerusalem, and we testify to it. Yet they put him to death, hanging him on a tree. 40God raised this same Jesus on the third day and allowed him to appear openly, 41though not to the whole people. He appeared to witnesses whom God had chosen ahead of time, to us. We ate and drank with him after he had risen from the dead. 42He gave us orders to announce this to the people and to declare solemnly that he is the one God has appointed as judge of the living and of the dead. 43Every one of the prophets bears witness to him: whoever believes in him has their sins forgiven through his name.”

The gift of the Spirit poured out on Gentiles

44Peter was still saying these things when the Holy Spirit came down on everyone who was listening to the message. 45The Jewish believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on Gentiles too. 46For they heard them speaking in tongues and praising the greatness of God. Then Peter said, 47“Surely no one can refuse the water to keep these people from being baptized. They have received the Holy Spirit just as we did!” 48So he gave orders for them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay on with them for a few days.
fields.summary: An angel tells Cornelius, a Roman centurion, to send for Peter, while Peter sees a vision teaching that what God has made clean is not to be called unclean. In Cornelius’s house Peter preaches that God does not favor one person over another, and the Holy Spirit is poured out on the Gentiles.

fields.title: Acts 11
fields.body_html:
Peter tells Jerusalem what happened in Caesarea

1Word reached the apostles and the brothers and sisters all over Judea that even the Gentiles had accepted the word of God. 2Once Peter was back in Jerusalem, the circumcised believers took him to task. 3“You went in to men who are uncircumcised,” they said, “and you sat down to eat with them!” 4Peter then explained everything to them step by step, from the beginning. 5“I was in the town of Joppa at prayer, and in a trance I had a vision. An object like a huge sheet, held at its four corners, was being lowered out of heaven, and it came all the way to me. 6As I stared into it and studied it closely, I saw animals of the earth that walk on four feet, wild animals, creatures that creep along the ground, and birds of the air. 7Then I also heard a voice speaking to me: ‘Up, Peter! Kill and eat.’ 8But I answered, ‘Certainly not, Lord! Nothing unholy or unclean has ever passed my lips.’ 9A second time the voice spoke from heaven: ‘What God has made clean, you must not call unholy.’ 10Three times this took place, and then everything was drawn back up into heaven. 11At that very moment three men reached the house where we were. They had been sent to me from Caesarea. 12The Spirit told me to go with them without making any distinction between them and us. These six brothers traveled with me as well, and we entered the man’s house. 13He described to us how he had seen the angel standing in his house, who said, ‘Send to Joppa and have Simon, also called Peter, brought here. 14He will speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and your whole household.’ 15I had only begun to speak when the Holy Spirit came down on them, just as the Spirit came on us at the start. 16Then the Lord’s words came back to me: ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ 17If, then, God gave them the same gift as he gave us when we came to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I? Could I hinder God?” 18At this they fell silent and glorified God. “Then God has given even the Gentiles repentance that brings life,” they said.

The good news reaches Antioch

19Meanwhile, the believers who had been scattered by the trouble that arose over Stephen made their way to Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch. They spoke the message to Jews and to no one else. 20Some of them, though, were from Cyprus and Cyrene. When they came to Antioch, they spoke to Greek-speaking Gentiles too and announced to them the good news of the Lord Jesus. 21The hand of the Lord was with them, and a large number who believed turned to the Lord. 22The church in Jerusalem got word of these things, and it sent Barnabas out to Antioch. 23On his arrival he saw the grace of God, and it made him glad. He kept urging everyone to hold fast to the Lord with firm resolve, 24for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a sizable crowd was added to the Lord. 25Barnabas then set out for Tarsus to search for Saul, 26and when he had found him he brought him to Antioch. For an entire year the two of them took part in the church’s gatherings and taught a sizable crowd. It was in Antioch that the disciples first came to be called Christians.

Agabus and the famine

27About that time prophets came down to Antioch from Jerusalem. 28Agabus, one of them, rose and, by the Spirit, foretold a great famine that would come on the whole world. And it came, in the days of the emperor Claudius. 29The disciples resolved that each of them would send something, as much as each could afford, as relief for the brothers and sisters living in Judea. 30And they carried it out, sending it to the elders in the care of Barnabas and Saul.
fields.summary: Peter tells the believers in Jerusalem what happened in Caesarea, and they praise God for giving repentance to the Gentiles. The good news reaches Antioch, where the disciples are first called Christians, and they send help to Judea in a famine.

fields.title: Acts 12
fields.body_html:
Herod kills James and seizes Peter

1At about that time King Herod moved against some of the church’s people, meaning to do them harm. 2He executed James, John’s brother, with the sword. 3When he saw how this pleased the Jews, he went further and had Peter taken too. It was the time of the Feast of Unleavened Bread. 4Once Peter was seized, Herod put him in prison and handed him over to four squads of four soldiers to keep guard. His plan was to bring him out before the people when the Passover was over. 5So Peter was under guard in the prison, but the church was praying to God for him without letup.

An angel leads Peter out of prison

6On the night before Herod was going to bring him out, Peter lay asleep between two soldiers, fastened with two chains, while guards in front of the door kept watch over the prison. 7All at once an angel of the Lord was standing there, and light filled the cell. He struck Peter’s side and woke him: “Up, quickly!” And the chains dropped from his hands. 8The angel told him, “Fasten your belt and put your sandals on.” Peter did as he was told. Then he said, “Wrap yourself in your cloak and come after me.” 9So Peter went out and followed. He did not know that the things the angel was doing were real; he took it all for a vision. 10They went past the first guard post and then the second, and came to the iron gate that opened onto the city. It swung open for them of its own accord. Out they went and on along one street, and suddenly the angel was gone from him. 11Then Peter came to himself. “Now I know for certain,” he said, “that the Lord sent his angel and snatched me out of Herod’s grasp and from all that the Jewish people were waiting to see.”

Rhoda at the gate

12When he had grasped this, he made his way to the home of Mary, mother of John whose other name was Mark.
