A good number of people had come together there and were praying. 13He knocked at the door in the gateway, and a servant girl named Rhoda came to see who it was. 14She knew Peter’s voice, and in her joy she left the gate shut. She ran inside and told them that Peter was standing at the gate. 15They said to her, “You have lost your mind!” But she held firmly that it was true. So they said, “It is his angel.” 16Peter, though, did not stop knocking. They opened the gate, saw him, and were beside themselves. 17He waved his hand to hush them and told them how the Lord had led him out of the prison. “Let James and the brothers and sisters know about this,” he said. Then he departed and went somewhere else.

18At daybreak the soldiers were in great alarm: what had happened to Peter? 19Herod had a search made for him, and when Peter could not be found, he questioned the guards and ordered them led off to execution. Then he left Judea, went down to Caesarea, and spent time there.

The death of Herod

20Herod had been in a bitter quarrel with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came to him together, and after winning over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they sued for peace, for their land drew its food from the king’s lands. 21On the day that was set, Herod dressed in his royal robes, took his seat on the platform, and began to address them. 22The crowd kept shouting, “A god is speaking, not a human being!” 23At once an angel of the Lord struck him, since he had not given the glory to God; worms ate at him, and he died.

24But the word of God went on growing and spreading. 25Barnabas and Saul, once they had completed their service in Jerusalem, returned and took John, also called Mark, along with them.
fields.summary: Herod kills James and imprisons Peter, but an angel leads Peter out of prison to the house where Rhoda answers the gate. Herod accepts the people’s praise as a god and dies, and the word of God keeps growing.

fields.title: Acts 13
fields.body_html:
The Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul

1The church in Antioch had prophets and teachers among its members: Barnabas, Simeon known as Niger, Lucius the Cyrenian, Manaen, a childhood companion of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. 2While they were serving the Lord in worship and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set Barnabas and Saul apart for me, for the work I have called them to do.” 3Then, after more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on the two men and let them go.

The proconsul and the magician on Cyprus

4So, sent out by the Holy Spirit, the two went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. 5Arriving at Salamis, they began to proclaim the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. They also had John with them as an assistant. 6They went across the whole island as far as Paphos, and there they came upon a Jewish magician, a false prophet, whose name was Bar-Jesus. 7He was in the company of the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding. The proconsul sent for Barnabas and Saul and asked to hear the word of God. 8But the magician Elymas, for that is how his name is translated, kept opposing them and tried to steer the proconsul away from the faith. 9Then Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fixed his eyes on him 10and said, “You are full of every kind of deceit and villainy, you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness! Will you never stop twisting the straight paths of the Lord? 11Now look: the hand of the Lord is against you. You will be blind and unable to see the sun for a while.” At once a mist and a darkness came down on him, and he moved about looking for someone to lead him by the hand. 12The proconsul, seeing what had taken place, believed. He was struck with amazement at the teaching about the Lord.

Paul speaks in the synagogue at Antioch

13Paul and those with him put out to sea from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. But John left them there and went back to Jerusalem. 14They went on from Perga and arrived at Antioch near Pisidia. On the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and took their seats. 15When the Law and the Prophets had been read, the leaders of the synagogue sent a message to them: “Brothers, if one of you has a word of encouragement for the people, speak.” 16Paul stood up, waved his hand for quiet, and said, “People of Israel, and you God-fearing Gentiles, listen. 17The God of this people Israel chose our ancestors. During their stay as foreigners in the land of Egypt he made the people great, and with a raised arm he led them out of that land. 18For about forty years he bore with their ways in the desert, 19and after he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave their land to his people to possess. 20The whole span was about 450 years. After that he gave them judges until the time of the prophet Samuel. 21Next they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, who reigned forty years. 22When he had set Saul aside, he raised up David to be their king, and he gave this testimony about him: ‘I have found David son of Jesse, a man in tune with my heart, who will carry out all that I want.’ 23From this man’s line God has brought Israel a Savior, Jesus, just as he promised. 24Before Jesus came, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. 25As John was finishing his course, he kept saying, ‘Who do you think I am? I am not the one. No, someone is coming after me, and I am not fit to untie the sandal on his feet.’

26Brothers and sisters, children of Abraham’s family, and you among us who fear God: this message of salvation has been sent out to us. 27The people of Jerusalem and their leaders did not know who he was, and they did not understand the words of the prophets that are read out every Sabbath; yet by condemning him they made those words come true. 28They found no charge that deserved death, and still they demanded that Pilate have him killed. 29When they had done everything that was written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. 30But God raised him from the dead, 31and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. They are now his witnesses to the people. 32And we are bringing you good news: the promise made to the ancestors 33God has now fulfilled for our children by raising up Jesus. So it stands written in the second psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ 34And that God raised him from the dead, never again to go back to decay, he declared in these words: ‘I will give you the holy blessings of David, the ones that can be trusted.’ 35That is why he also says in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One undergo decay.’ 36For David, after serving God’s purpose in his own generation, fell asleep in death; he was laid to rest with his ancestors, and his body decayed. 37But the one whom God raised up did not undergo decay. 38So, brothers and sisters, you must know this: through this man forgiveness of sins is being announced to you, and from everything the law of Moses could not acquit you of, 39everyone who believes is acquitted through him. 40So be careful, or what was said in the Prophets may come upon you: 41‘See, you who scorn, be astonished and vanish! For I am doing a work in your days, a work you would never believe, even if someone explained it to you.’”

42As Paul and Barnabas were going out, the people kept urging them to speak about these things again on the next Sabbath. 43After the gathering broke up, many Jews and converts who worshiped God went along with Paul and Barnabas, who talked with them and kept persuading them to remain in the grace of God.

The whole city gathers to hear

44The following Sabbath nearly the entire city came together to hear the word of the Lord. 45But when the Jews saw the crowds, jealousy filled them, and they spoke against what Paul was saying and reviled him. 46Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly: “The word of God had to be spoken to you first. Since you push it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, see, we are turning to the Gentiles. 47For this is the command the Lord has given us: ‘I have set you as a light for the nations, so that you may be the means of salvation to the farthest part of the earth.’” 48When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who had been appointed to eternal life believed. 49And the word of the Lord spread across the whole region. 50But the Jews stirred up the respected women who worshiped God and the leading men of the city; they started a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district. 51So the two shook the dust from their feet against them and went on to Iconium. 52And the disciples went on being filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
fields.summary: The Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul, who on Cyprus confront a magician before the proconsul. In the synagogue at Antioch Paul proclaims Jesus as the fulfillment of God’s promise, and when many reject the message, the apostles turn to the Gentiles.

fields.title: Acts 14
fields.body_html:
In Iconium

1In Iconium the two of them went together into the synagogue of the Jews. They spoke in such a way that a large crowd of Jews and Greeks believed. 2But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and turned their minds against the brothers and sisters. 3So they stayed there a long time and spoke boldly, relying on the Lord. He bore witness to the word of his grace by allowing signs and wonders to happen through their hands. 4The people of the city were split: some sided with the Jews, and others with the apostles. 5When Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, set out to abuse the apostles and stone them, 6the apostles learned of it and escaped to Lystra and Derbe, towns of Lycaonia, and to the country around them. 7There they kept on proclaiming the gospel.

Called gods at Lystra

8At Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He had been lame since birth and had never taken a step. 9The man was listening while Paul spoke. Paul fixed his eyes on him and saw that he had faith that he would be made well. 10So he said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet!” And the man leaped up and walked. 11When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices in the Lycaonian language: “The gods have become like humans and come down to us!” 12They began calling Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because Paul was the one who took the lead in speaking. 13Zeus had a temple just in front of the city. His priest came to the gates with bulls and garlands, for he and the crowds meant to offer sacrifice. 14But the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it. They ripped their garments and dashed into the middle of the crowd, crying out, 15“People, why are you doing these things? We are mortals with the same nature as you. We have come with the gospel, calling you to turn away from these empty things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything that is in them. 16In past generations he allowed every nation to walk in its own ways. 17Even so, he has not left himself without a witness. He does you good: he gives you rain from the sky and seasons that bear fruit, and he fills you with food and your hearts with gladness.” 18Saying these things, they could hardly hold the crowds back from offering sacrifice to them.

Paul stoned at Lystra

19But Jews from Antioch and Iconium came on the scene and persuaded the crowds. They stoned Paul and hauled him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. 20But when the disciples stood in a circle around him, he rose and went back into the city. The next day he set out with Barnabas for Derbe.

Back through the cities, and home to Antioch

21They proclaimed the gospel in that city and made many disciples. After that they retraced their steps to Lystra, to Iconium and to Antioch. 22They made the disciples strong in spirit and urged them to hold on to the faith, saying, “We must enter the kingdom of God by way of many afflictions.” 23In each church they appointed elders for the believers, and after praying and fasting, they placed them in the care of the Lord in whom they had believed. 24They crossed Pisidia and came into Pamphylia, 25and when they had spoken the word in Perga they went down to Attalia. 26From there they set sail for Antioch, the place where they had first been entrusted to God’s grace for the task that they had now carried out to the end. 27Once they had arrived, they called the church together and told all that God had done as he worked along with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. 28And they remained a long while with the disciples there.
fields.summary: In Iconium many believe, but the apostles must flee. At Lystra the crowd calls Paul and Barnabas gods after a lame man is healed, then Paul is stoned and left for dead, and the two return through the cities to Antioch.

fields.title: Acts 15
fields.body_html:
The question of circumcision

1Some people came down from Judea and began teaching the brothers and sisters, “Unless you are circumcised as the custom of Moses requires, there is no way for you to be saved.” 2This led to fierce dispute and argument between them and Paul and Barnabas. So it was arranged that Paul and Barnabas and some others from among them should go up to Jerusalem and put this question to the apostles and the elders. 3The church sent them off, and as they went through Phoenicia and Samaria they told in full how the Gentiles were turning to God. The news brought great joy to all the brothers and sisters. 4On reaching Jerusalem they were received by the church, the apostles and the elders, and they told them everything God had done in company with them. 5Then some from the party of the Pharisees who had believed stood up and insisted, “These Gentiles have to be circumcised, and they must be ordered to keep the law of Moses.”

The apostles and the elders consider the matter

6The apostles and the elders came together to consider this matter. 7After a long debate, Peter rose and spoke to them: “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made his choice among you: through my mouth the Gentiles were to hear the message of the gospel and come to believe. 8God, who knows every heart, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, as he did for us as well. 9He made no difference at all between us and them, for he cleansed their hearts by faith. 10So why are you now putting God to the test? You would lay on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither our ancestors nor we ourselves have had the strength to carry. 11No, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, and they are saved in just the same way.”

12The whole gathering grew quiet. Everyone listened to Barnabas and Paul as they told of the signs and wonders God had worked among the Gentiles through them. 13When they had finished, James responded, “Brothers, listen to what I have to say. 14Simeon has explained how God first looked with favor on the Gentiles, to take from among them a people to bear his name. 15What the prophets said agrees with this, as it stands written: 16‘After this I will come back, and I will build again the fallen tent of David. I will build again its ruins and raise it up once more, 17so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord, all the nations that are called by my name, says the Lord, who does these things, 18things made known long ago.’ 19So my judgment is that we should not make things hard for the Gentiles who are turning to God. 20Instead we should write to them that they keep away from what idols have defiled, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood. 21For Moses has been preached in every town since generations long past, and he is read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

A letter to the Gentile believers

22Then the apostles and the elders, together with the whole church, decided to pick men from among themselves and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They chose Judas, known as Barsabbas, and Silas, men who held leading places among the brothers and sisters. 23They sent with them this letter: “From the apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers and sisters of Gentile birth in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia: greetings. 24We have heard that some who went out from us have disturbed you with what they said and left you unsettled, though we gave them no such instructions. 25So we have come to one mind and decided to choose men and send them to you with Barnabas and Paul, whom we love, 26men who have given their lives over for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. 27So we are sending Judas and Silas, who will tell you the same things in person. 28The Holy Spirit and we ourselves have decided to place on you no burden beyond these essentials: 29keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you guard yourselves against these, you will be doing what is right. Farewell.”

30So the men were sent on their way and went down to Antioch. There they called the whole community together and handed over the letter. 31When they had read it, they were glad for the encouragement it brought. 32Judas and Silas, who were also prophets, spoke at length to encourage the brothers and sisters and to make them strong. 33After they had stayed there for some time, the brothers and sisters let them go in peace, back to those who had sent them. 35Paul and Barnabas, though, stayed on in Antioch. Along with many others, they taught the word of the Lord and proclaimed it as good news.

Paul and Barnabas go separate ways

36Some days later Paul said to Barnabas, “Come, let us go back and look in on the brothers and sisters in every town where we announced the word of the Lord, and find out how they are doing.” 37Barnabas wanted to bring John, also called Mark, with them too. 38But Paul did not think it right to take with them a man who had left them in Pamphylia and had not gone on with them to the work. 39The quarrel grew so heated that the two of them parted ways. Barnabas took Mark and sailed off to Cyprus, 40while Paul picked Silas and set out, after the brothers and sisters had commended him to the grace of the Lord. 41He traveled through Syria and Cilicia, making the churches strong.
fields.summary: In Jerusalem the apostles and elders consider whether Gentile believers must be circumcised, and James proposes that they need not. A letter is sent to the Gentile believers, and Paul and Barnabas go separate ways after a sharp disagreement.

fields.title: Acts 16
fields.body_html:
Timothy joins Paul and Silas

1Paul came to Derbe and then on to Lystra. A disciple called Timothy was living there. His mother was a Jewish woman who believed, but his father was a Greek. 2The brothers and sisters in Lystra and Iconium thought highly of him. 3Paul wanted to have Timothy with him when he set out. With the Jews of that area in mind, he took him and circumcised him, since all of them knew that his father was a Greek. 4As they made their way from town to town, they passed on to the believers the decisions reached by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, for them to observe. 5So the churches grew firmer in the faith, and their numbers rose day by day.

The call from Macedonia

6They went on through the Phrygian and Galatian country, because the Holy Spirit had stopped them from speaking the word in Asia. 7Coming as far as Mysia, they made an attempt to go on into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit it. 8So they skirted Mysia and went down to Troas. 9In the night Paul saw a vision. A man of Macedonia stood there and pleaded with him, “Cross over to Macedonia and help us!” 10As soon as he had seen the vision, we looked for a way to set out for Macedonia, sure now that God had called us to bring the gospel to its people.

Lydia at the place of prayer

11So we set sail from Troas and ran with a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day reached Neapolis. 12From there we made our way to Philippi, which ranks as a leading city of its district of Macedonia and is a Roman colony. We spent several days in that city. 13On the Sabbath day we went out beyond the gate, beside a river, where we thought there might be a place of prayer. We took a seat and spoke to the women who had come together. 14A woman named Lydia was listening, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God. The Lord opened her heart to heed what Paul was saying. 15After she and her household had been baptized, she pressed us to accept her offer: “If you are satisfied that I am faithful to the Lord, come into my home and stay.” And she would not take no for an answer.

A slave girl with a spirit of Python

16Once, on our way to the place of prayer, a slave girl came to meet us who had a soothsaying spirit. Her fortune-telling brought in a large income for her masters. 17She trailed after Paul and the rest of us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, and they are announcing to you a way of salvation!” 18She kept this up for many days. In the end Paul grew weary and vexed. He turned and told the spirit, “I order you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It came out that same hour.

19Her masters saw that their hope of gain had gone out of her along with the spirit. So they laid hold of Paul and Silas and hauled them off to the rulers in the marketplace. 20Bringing them before the magistrates, they said, “These men are upsetting our whole city. They are Jews, 21and they preach customs that we cannot lawfully take up or follow, since we are Romans.” 22The crowd too rose up against them, and the magistrates tore the clothes off them and ordered them beaten with rods. 23When they had struck them many blows, they threw them into prison and told the jailer to keep them safely locked up. 24Given such a charge, the jailer threw them into the inner part of the prison and made their feet fast in the stocks.

Midnight in the prison at Philippi

25At midnight, as Paul and Silas prayed, they sang praises to God, and the prisoners listened. 26All at once a great earthquake struck, so strong that the prison was shaken to its foundations. In that instant all the doors came open, and the chains of every prisoner fell loose. 27Startled out of sleep, the jailer saw that the prison doors stood open. Believing that the prisoners had got away, he drew his sword, ready to take his own life. 28But Paul shouted at the top of his voice, “Do not hurt yourself! Every one of us is still here!” 29He called for lights and ran inside, and shaking with fear he fell at the feet of Paul and Silas. 30He led them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” 31They answered, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” 32And they shared the word of the Lord with him and with everyone in his household. 33Even at that hour of the night he took them and bathed their wounds, and straightaway he was baptized together with all his family. 34Leading them up into his house, he spread a table for them, and the whole household rejoiced with him, now that he had believed in God.

Roman citizens released

35In the morning the magistrates sent their lictors with the order, “Let those men go.” 36The jailer passed the message on to Paul: “The magistrates have sent orders for your release. So come out now, and go in peace.” 37But Paul told them, “We are Roman citizens, and they beat us in front of everyone without condemning us in any court, and threw us into prison. Are they now going to send us away in secret? Certainly not! Let them come in person and lead us out.” 38The lictors carried these words back to the magistrates, who were frightened to hear that the men were Roman citizens. 39They came and pleaded with them, and after leading them out, they kept asking them to leave the city. 40So they came out of the prison and went to Lydia. They saw the brothers and sisters and encouraged them, and then they set out.
fields.summary: Timothy joins Paul and Silas, and a vision calls them to Macedonia. In Philippi Lydia believes, a slave girl is freed from a spirit, and after an earthquake at midnight the jailer and his household are baptized; the magistrates release Paul and Silas, who are Roman citizens.

fields.title: Acts 17
fields.body_html:
Reasoning from the Scriptures in Thessalonica

1They traveled on through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where the Jews had a synagogue. 2As he usually did, Paul went to the synagogue, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, 3opening them up and laying out the case that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I am proclaiming to you,” he said, “is the Christ.” 4Some of the Jews were convinced and threw in their lot with Paul and Silas, as did a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few of the city’s leading women. 5But the Jews grew jealous. They rounded up some troublemakers from the marketplace, gathered a mob and threw the city into an uproar. They stormed Jason’s house, looking for Paul and Silas to bring them out before the people. 6When they could not find them, they hauled Jason and some of the brothers and sisters before the city officials, shouting, “These men who have stirred up trouble all over the world have now come here, 7and Jason has taken them into his home! They all defy Caesar’s decrees and say there is another king, one called Jesus.” 8Hearing this, the crowd and the city officials were thrown into alarm. 9They made Jason and the others post a bond, and then let them go.

Berea examines the Scriptures

10That same night the brothers and sisters lost no time in sending Paul and Silas off to Berea. When they got there, they went to the Jewish synagogue. 11The Jews here were more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica. They took in the message with real eagerness and went through the Scriptures day after day to check whether what Paul said was true. 12So many of them believed, along with a good number of Greek women of standing, and of men as well. 13But when the Jews of Thessalonica found out that Paul was proclaiming the word of God in Berea as well, they came there too, unsettling the crowds and stirring up trouble. 14At once the brothers and sisters sent Paul off toward the coast, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind. 15The men escorting Paul took him all the way to Athens. Then they set off back with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as they could.

A city full of idols

16While Paul waited for them in Athens, he was deeply troubled in spirit to see the city crowded with idols. 17So he argued in the synagogue with the Jews and the God-fearing Gentiles, and every day in the marketplace with anyone who happened to come by. 18Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also took him on in debate. Some of them said, “What is this scrap-collector of ideas trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be promoting foreign gods.” They said this because he was announcing the good news about Jesus and the resurrection. 19They took him and brought him before the Areopagus. “May we know,” they said, “what this new teaching of yours is? 20Some of the things we hear from you sound strange to us, and we would like to know what they mean.” 21(All the Athenians, and the foreigners who lived there, spent their leisure on nothing but telling or hearing the latest new idea.)

To an unknown god

22Paul stood up in front of the Areopagus and said: “People of Athens, I can see that in every respect you are extremely religious. 23As I walked around and looked closely at the things you worship, I even came upon an altar with this inscription: ‘To an unknown god.’ So what you worship without knowing it, I now make known to you. 24God, who made the world and all that is in it, is himself Lord of heaven and earth. He does not dwell in shrines that hands have made. 25Nor do human hands wait on him as if he lacked anything, since it is he who gives life and breath and all things to everyone. 26From one ancestor he made every nation of humankind to live over the whole face of the earth. He fixed the times set for them and the bounds of the places where they would live, 27so that they would seek God and perhaps grope their way toward him and find him. And yet he is not far away from any of us. 28It is in him that we live and move and exist. As some of your own poets have also put it, ‘We too are his offspring.’ 29If we are God’s offspring, then, we must not suppose that the divine nature resembles gold, silver or stone, carved into shape by human art and invention. 30God has passed over those times of ignorance, but now he orders people everywhere, all of them, to repent, 31because he has fixed a day on which he is going to judge the world in righteousness through a man he has appointed. And he has given everyone a pledge of this by raising him from the dead.”

32When they heard about the raising of the dead, some scoffed, while others said, “We will listen to you on this another time.” 33With that, Paul went out from among them. 34But some people attached themselves to him and believed. Among them were Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus council, a woman called Damaris, and others besides.
fields.summary: Paul reasons from the Scriptures in Thessalonica, and the people of Berea examine the Scriptures daily. In Athens, a city full of idols, Paul speaks at the Areopagus about the unknown god who made the world and raised Jesus from the dead.

fields.title: Acts 18
fields.body_html:
Paul comes to Corinth

1After this, Paul left Athens and went on to Corinth. 2There he met a Jew called Aquila, born in Pontus, who had lately arrived from Italy with his wife Priscilla, since Claudius had ordered every Jew to leave Rome. Paul went to see them, 3and because he and they worked at the same craft, he stayed in their home and worked with them. By trade they were tentmakers. 4Each Sabbath he debated in the synagogue, seeking to win over Jews and Greeks alike.

A year and a half in Corinth

5Once Silas and Timothy had come down from Macedonia, Paul gave himself fully to the word, bearing witness to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. 6But they set themselves against him and spoke abusively, so he shook out his clothes and said to them, “Your blood is on your own heads. I am clear of it. From now on I am going to the Gentiles.” 7Paul left them and went over to the home of a man named Titius Justus, who worshiped God. His house stood right beside the synagogue. 8Crispus, who led the synagogue, believed in the Lord, and so did everyone in his household. Many other people in Corinth heard the message, believed and were baptized. 9In a vision at night the Lord told Paul, “Stop being afraid. Go on speaking, and do not fall silent. 10I am with you. No one will lay a hand on you to hurt you, because many in this city belong to me.” 11Paul stayed on for eighteen months, teaching the word of God among them. 12But while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews joined forces against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat. 13Their charge was this: “He is talking people into worshiping God in a way the law does not allow.” 14Paul was about to speak when Gallio said to the Jews, “If this were some wrong or a serious crime, you Jews, I would have good reason to take up your case. 15But these are disputes over teaching and titles and your own law. Deal with them yourselves. I will not sit in judgment on matters like these.” 16Then he had them driven away from the judgment seat. 17Then they all grabbed Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But Gallio paid no attention to any of it.

Back to Antioch, and Apollos in Ephesus

18Paul remained many days longer. Then he took leave of the brothers and sisters and sailed for Syria, and Priscilla and Aquila went with him. In Cenchreae he had his head shaved, since he had made a vow. 19They arrived at Ephesus, where Paul was to leave Priscilla and Aquila. He went into the synagogue on his own and debated with the Jews. 20They urged him to stay longer, but he would not agree. 21As he said goodbye, he told them, “I will come back to you, if God wills,” and he put out to sea from Ephesus. 22He came ashore at Caesarea, went up to greet the church, and then went down to Antioch. 23After some time there he set out again and journeyed through the Galatian country and Phrygia, town after town, building up all the disciples. 24A Jew called Apollos, born in Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was a gifted speaker and could handle the Scriptures with power. 25He had been taught the way of the Lord, and with great zeal he spoke and taught the facts about Jesus correctly, though the only baptism he knew was John’s. 26He started to speak out fearlessly in the synagogue. Priscilla and Aquila heard him there, and they took him in and taught him the way of God more precisely. 27Apollos planned to go across to Achaia, and the brothers and sisters encouraged him in it. They wrote to the disciples there, asking them to welcome him. Once he came, he gave much help to those who had come to believe through grace, 28for he argued powerfully and publicly against the Jews, proving them wrong, and used the Scriptures to show that Jesus is the Christ.
fields.summary: In Corinth Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla and stays a year and a half, encouraged by a vision, while Gallio refuses to hear the case against him. Paul returns to Antioch, and in Ephesus Apollos is taught the way of God more accurately.

fields.title: Acts 19
fields.body_html:
Disciples who knew only John’s baptism

1While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul made his way through the inland regions and came down to Ephesus. There he came upon some disciples 2and asked them, “When you came to believe, did you receive the Holy Spirit?” They told him, “No. We never even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.” 3Paul asked, “Then into what were you baptized?” “Into John’s baptism,” they answered. 4Paul said, “The baptism John performed marked people’s repentance, and he told the people to believe in the one who would come after him, namely Jesus.” 5When they heard this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. 6Then as Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them. They began speaking in tongues and prophesying. 7In all, the men numbered about twelve.

Two years in the hall of Tyrannus

8Paul went into the synagogue, and for three months he spoke there without fear, debating and trying to win people over about the kingdom of God. 9Some, though, hardened themselves and refused to be persuaded, and they spoke against the Way in front of the gathering. Paul then withdrew from them, taking the disciples apart with him, and each day he held discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. 10This carried on for two years, with the result that all the people of the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.

The sons of Sceva and the books of magic

11God worked miracles of no common kind through Paul’s hands, 12so that people would even take cloths and work aprons that had touched his skin to those who were ill. Their sicknesses left them, and the evil spirits came out. 13There were also some Jewish exorcists who traveled from town to town, and they tried calling on the name of the Lord Jesus over people who had evil spirits. “I charge you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches,” they would say. 14A Jewish high priest named Sceva had seven sons who were doing this. 15The evil spirit answered them, “I know Jesus, and I am acquainted with Paul. But you, who are you?” 16Then the man who had the evil spirit threw himself on them. He mastered every one of them and was too strong for them, so that they fled from that house stripped of their clothes and covered with wounds. 17Everyone in Ephesus, Jews and Greeks alike, came to hear of this. Fear took hold of them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was more and more honored. 18Many who had believed began coming forward to confess and to disclose their practices. 19A good number of those who had practiced magic collected their books and burned them where everyone could see. When the value of the books was added up, it came to 50,000 silver coins. 20So with great power the word of the Lord kept growing and gaining strength.

21After these events, Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go on to Jerusalem. “Once I have been there,” he said, “I must see Rome as well.” 22Paul sent Timothy and Erastus, two of the men who assisted him, on to Macedonia, but he remained in the province of Asia for some time longer.

Great is Artemis of the Ephesians

23Around that time a serious uproar broke out over the Way. 24There was a silversmith named Demetrius who made silver shrines of Artemis, and he provided plenty of work for the craftsmen. 25He gathered them, and the workers in trades like theirs, and told them, “Men, you know well that our wealth comes from this work. 26You also see and hear what this Paul is doing. Not only in Ephesus, but across nearly the whole of Asia, he has won over a large crowd and drawn them away by telling them that anything made with hands is no god. 27It is not only that our trade risks being despised. The temple of the great goddess Artemis may come to count for nothing, and she, the goddess whom all Asia and the whole world worship, may soon be pulled down from her greatness.”

28On hearing this they flew into a rage, and they kept shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” 29Confusion spread through the city, and with one impulse the people stormed into the theater, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, the Macedonians who traveled with Paul. 30Paul was ready to go in and face the assembled people, but the disciples kept him from doing so. 31Some of the Asiarchs, too, who were his friends, sent word to him and pleaded with him not to put himself at risk in the theater. 32Meanwhile people shouted all kinds of things, some one thing and some another. The assembly was in chaos, and most of them had no idea what had brought them there. 33Some of the crowd told Alexander what to say, since the Jews had pushed him forward, and Alexander signaled with his hand, intending to speak in his own defense to the people. 34But as soon as they realized he was a Jew, they all joined in one shout, and for about two hours they cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” 35The town clerk managed to quiet the crowd and said, “People of Ephesus, is there anyone at all who does not know that this city of the Ephesians has been entrusted with the temple of the great Artemis and with the image that fell from heaven? 36No one can dispute these facts, so you ought to keep calm and not do anything reckless. 37These men you have dragged here are not temple robbers, and they have not insulted our goddess. 38So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a case against anyone, there are court days and there are proconsuls; let the parties bring their charges against each other there. 39Any further matter you raise will be dealt with in the lawful assembly. 40–41Indeed, today’s events put us in danger of being accused of rebellion. There is no cause we could point to, nothing we could say to explain this disorderly gathering.” With these words he sent the assembly away.
fields.summary: In Ephesus Paul baptizes disciples who knew only John’s baptism and teaches for two years in the hall of Tyrannus. The sons of Sceva are overpowered, believers burn their books of magic, and the silversmiths stir up a riot in honor of Artemis of the Ephesians.

fields.title: Acts 20
fields.body_html:
Through Macedonia and Greece

1When the uproar had died down, Paul sent for the disciples and encouraged them. Then he said goodbye and set out for Macedonia. 2He went through those parts, speaking at length to the disciples to encourage them, and came to Greece. 3He stayed there three months. Just as he was about to sail for Syria, the Jews laid a plot against him, so he made up his mind to go back through Macedonia. 4He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from the province of Asia. 5These men went on ahead and waited for us at Troas. 6We ourselves sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and five days later we joined them at Troas. We spent seven days there.

Eutychus at Troas

7On the first day of the week we met together to break bread. Paul spoke with the people there, because he intended to leave the next day, and his talk went on until midnight. 8There were plenty of lamps in the upstairs room where we had gathered. 9A young man named Eutychus sat in the window opening. Paul’s talk ran longer and longer, and Eutychus sank into a heavy sleep. Overcome by it, he fell from the third floor to the ground, and when they lifted him up he was dead. 10Paul went down, threw himself on the young man, and held him close. “Do not be upset,” he said, “his life is in him.” 11Then he went back upstairs, broke the bread and ate. He went on talking with them a long time, until dawn, and then he left. 12They led the boy away alive, and they were greatly comforted.

From Troas to Miletus

13We went on ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, where we meant to take Paul on board. He had arranged it this way, because he wanted to go there on foot. 14When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went on to Mitylene. 15We sailed from there and the next day arrived off Chios. The day after that we crossed to Samos, and a day later we reached Miletus. 16Paul had decided to sail on past Ephesus so as not to lose time in the province of Asia. He was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if he could, by the day of Pentecost.

Paul speaks to the elders of Ephesus

17From Miletus he sent word to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. 18When they had come, he said to them, “From the first day I set foot in the province of Asia, you have seen what kind of life I led among you the whole time. 19I worked as the Lord’s servant, with all humility and with tears, enduring the trials that the plots of the Jews brought on me. 20You know how I held back nothing that was for your good, but made it known to you and taught you, in public and from house to house. 21To Jews and Greeks alike I bore solemn witness about repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus. 22And now, bound by the Spirit, I am on my way to Jerusalem. What I will meet there I do not know, 23except that in one city after another the Holy Spirit bears witness to me that chains and hardships lie ahead of me. 24But I set no value on my life, as if it were precious to me. All I want is to run my course to the end and carry out the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus: to bear full witness to the gospel of the grace of God.

25And now I know this: you will not see my face again, not one of you among whom I have gone from place to place proclaiming the kingdom. 26So on this day I solemnly tell you: I am free from guilt for anyone’s blood. 27I never drew back from making known to you God’s whole plan. 28Be on your guard, for yourselves and for the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers to shepherd the church of God, which he won for himself through his own blood. 29Once I have gone, I know, savage wolves will force their way in among you, with no mercy for the flock. 30And from your own ranks people will stand up and speak twisted things, to lure the disciples into following them. 31So be watchful, and remember: for three years I did not stop, night or day, admonishing each one of you with tears. 32And now I place you in the care of God and of the message of his grace. That message has power to build you up and to give you your share among all who have been made holy. 33I never set my heart on anyone’s silver or gold or clothing. 34You know yourselves that I provided for my own needs, and for those who were with me, with these hands. 35In every way I set you an example: by working hard like this we must come to the aid of the weak, and keep in mind the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

Farewell at Miletus

36After saying this, he knelt down and prayed with them all. 37They all wept freely. They threw their arms around Paul and kissed him again and again. 38Above all, they were pained by what he had said, that they would not see his face any more. Then they went with him down to the ship.
fields.summary: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, and at Troas raises Eutychus, who fell from a window. At Miletus Paul speaks to the elders of Ephesus, urging them to shepherd the church, and they part in tears.

fields.title: Acts 21
fields.body_html:
The voyage to Tyre

1When we had parted from them, hard as it was, and put out to sea, we made a straight run to Cos. The next day we came to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. 2There we found a ship bound across the sea for Phoenicia, so we went aboard and put out. 3We came in sight of Cyprus and passed it by on our left, sailing on toward Syria, and we put in at Tyre, because the ship was to discharge its cargo there. 4We looked up the disciples there and stayed seven days. Speaking through the Spirit, they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. 5When our time there came to an end, we set out on our way again. The whole company, wives and children too, walked with us until we were outside the city. On the shore we went down on our knees and prayed, 6and we took leave of one another. Then we boarded the ship, and they went back to their homes.

In the house of Philip at Caesarea

7We brought the voyage from Tyre to its end at Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and sisters and spent a day with them. 8The next day we left and came to Caesarea. We made our way to the house of Philip the evangelist, who had been one of the seven, and stayed as his guests. 9Philip had four daughters who were not married, and they prophesied. 10During our stay of several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. 11He came to us, took Paul’s belt, and bound his own feet and hands with it. He said, “Here is what the Holy Spirit says: ‘Like this the Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man this belt belongs to, and they will give him up into the hands of the Gentiles.’” 12At these words, we ourselves joined the people of the place in urging Paul again and again not to go up to Jerusalem. 13Paul replied, “What do you mean by weeping and crushing my heart? For my part, I am prepared to be bound in Jerusalem, and more than that, to die there, for the name of the Lord Jesus.” 14Since he would not be persuaded, we said no more except, “Let the Lord’s will be done.”

15After those days we got our things ready and set out on the road up to Jerusalem. 16Some of the disciples from Caesarea came along with us. They took us to the house of Mnason, a man of Cyprus and a disciple from the early days, so that we could stay with him.

Paul with James and the elders

17When we came to Jerusalem, the brothers and sisters were glad to welcome us. 18On the day after, Paul took us with him to James, and the elders all came. 19After greeting them, Paul told them, item by item, everything God had accomplished among the Gentiles through the service he had been given. 20On hearing this they glorified God, and they said to Paul, “Look, brother, at the tens of thousands of believers there are among the Jews, and every one of them is deeply devoted to the law. 21Yet word has reached them that you are teaching the Jews scattered among the Gentiles to abandon Moses, and that you say they should no longer circumcise their children or follow the customs. 22So what is to be done? There is no doubt they will hear that you have arrived. 23Here is our advice, then. Four men among us have taken a vow on themselves. 24Bring these men with you, be purified along with them, and cover the cost of their offerings so that they can shave their heads. Then everyone will see that the reports about you are empty, and that you yourself live in line with the law and keep it. 25For the Gentiles who have come to believe, we have already written what we decided: they are to avoid meat sacrificed to idols, and blood, and anything strangled, and sexual immorality.” 26Then Paul took the men along. On the following day he was purified with them and went into the temple, announcing when their days of purification would be over and the offering for each of them would be presented.

Seized in the temple

27The seven days were nearly over when some Jews from Asia caught sight of Paul in the temple. They threw the whole crowd into confusion and laid hands on him, 28shouting, “People of Israel, help! This is the man whose teaching, everywhere he goes, sets everyone against our people, the law and this place. And now he has even brought Greeks into the temple and made this holy place unclean.” 29For they had seen Paul in the city a little earlier with Trophimus, a man of Ephesus, and they took it for granted that Paul had taken him into the temple. 30The entire city was set in motion, and the people rushed together. They laid hold of Paul and hauled him out of the temple, and straightaway the gates were closed. 31They were set on killing him when a report went up to the tribune in command of the cohort that the whole of Jerusalem was in turmoil. 32He immediately took soldiers and centurions and rushed down on the crowd, and at the sight of the tribune and the soldiers they left off beating Paul. 33Coming up to Paul, the tribune took him into custody and gave orders to fasten him with two chains. He began asking who the man was and what he had been doing. 34But the crowd shouted back, some one thing, some another. The din made it impossible for him to get at the facts, so he had Paul taken into the barracks. 35At the stairs, the crowd’s violence was such that the soldiers had to carry Paul up. 36The whole mass of people came after them, crying out, “Away with him!”

Paul asks to speak to the people

37As they were about to take him into the barracks, Paul said to the tribune, “May I have a word with you?” The tribune said, “You know Greek? 38So you are not the Egyptian who stirred up a rebellion a while ago and led the 4,000 men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?” 39Paul answered, “I am a Jew, a man of Tarsus in Cilicia, and a citizen of a city of some note. I ask you, allow me to address the people.” 40The tribune gave permission, and Paul, standing on the steps, raised his hand to the people. When all had fallen silent, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language. He said:
fields.summary: Paul sails to Tyre and Caesarea, where Agabus warns that Paul will be bound in Jerusalem. Paul meets with James and the elders, but in the temple a crowd seizes Paul, and the Roman tribune allows Paul to speak to the people.

fields.title: Acts 22
fields.body_html:
Paul’s defense to the people of Jerusalem

1“Brothers and fathers, listen now to the defense I am making before you.”

2When they heard him speaking to them in Hebrew, they grew even quieter. Then he went on: 3“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia but raised here in this city. I sat at the feet of Gamaliel and was trained with great precision in our ancestral law. I was as zealous for God as every one of you is today. 4I persecuted this Way to the point of death, putting men and women alike in chains and handing them over to prison. 5The high priest himself can confirm this, and so can the whole council of elders. I even got letters from them to our fellow Jews in Damascus, and I set off to bring the people there back to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.

A light from heaven near Damascus

6As I was traveling and coming close to Damascus, at about midday, all at once a brilliant light from heaven blazed around me. 7I dropped to the ground and heard a voice say to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’ 8‘Who are you, Lord?’ I answered. He told me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, the one you are persecuting.’ 9My companions saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me. 10I asked, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ The Lord answered, ‘Get up and go on into Damascus. There you will be told all that has been assigned for you to do.’ 11Because the glory of that light had left me unable to see, my companions led me by the hand, and I came into Damascus. 12There was a man named Ananias, devout in keeping the law and well regarded by all the Jews who lived there. 13He came and stood beside me and said, ‘Brother Saul, see again!’ In that very moment my sight came back, and I looked up at him. 14Then he said, ‘The God of our ancestors has chosen you beforehand to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear words from his own mouth. 15You will be his witness to everyone, telling what you have seen and heard. 16Now why wait any longer? Get up and be baptized. Let your sins be washed away as you call on his name.’

A trance in the temple

17After I had come back to Jerusalem, I was praying in the temple when I fell into a trance. 18I saw the Lord, and he said to me, ‘Hurry! Leave Jerusalem at once, for the people here will not accept what you tell them about me.’ 19I answered, ‘Lord, these people know well what I did. In one synagogue after another I had those who believe in you locked up and beaten. 20When Stephen, your witness, was put to death and his blood poured out, I was there myself. I agreed with what they did, and I looked after the cloaks of those who killed him.’ 21Then he told me, ‘Go! I am going to send you far away, to the Gentiles.’”

A Roman citizen by birth

22The crowd heard him out until he said this. Then they raised a shout: “Take a man like this off the face of the earth! He should never have been allowed to live!” 23They kept yelling, flinging off their cloaks and tossing dust into the air. 24So the tribune ordered Paul taken into the barracks. He gave orders for him to be questioned under the whip, to find out why the people were shouting at him so. 25They had stretched him out and tied him with straps when Paul said to the centurion on duty, “Does the law allow you to flog a Roman citizen, and one who has had no trial?” 26When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and told him, “What is this you are about to do? This man is a Roman citizen!” 27The tribune came over and asked him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” “Yes,” he said. 28The tribune replied, “It cost me a great deal of money to get this citizenship.” Paul answered, “And I am one by birth.” 29At once the men who were going to question him backed away. The tribune, too, grew afraid once he learned that Paul was a Roman citizen, since he had had him tied up.

Brought before the council

30On the following day, since the tribune wanted to learn the true reason for the charges the Jews were bringing against Paul, he freed him from his chains. He summoned the chief priests and the full council, then brought Paul down and placed him in front of them.
fields.summary: Paul tells the people of Jerusalem how the light from heaven stopped him near Damascus and how in a trance in the temple the Lord sent him to the Gentiles. The crowd erupts, and Paul, about to be flogged, says he is a Roman citizen by birth and is brought before the council.

fields.title: Acts 23
fields.body_html:
Paul before the council

1Paul fixed his eyes on the council and said, “Brothers, I have conducted my life before God with a fully clear conscience up to this very day.” 2At that, Ananias the high priest told the men standing near Paul to hit him in the mouth. 3Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you in turn, you whitewashed wall! You are seated to try me by the law, and you break that same law by having me hit?” 4Those standing by said, “You insult God’s own high priest?” 5Paul answered, “Brothers, I was not aware that he was the high priest. For Scripture says, ‘Never speak ill of one who rules your people.’”

6Aware that the council was made up partly of Sadducees and partly of Pharisees, Paul called out to them, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, born to a family of Pharisees. It is over the hope of the dead rising that I am on trial.” 7As soon as he said this, the Pharisees and Sadducees began to quarrel, and the gathering split in two. 8The Sadducees say there is no resurrection, and neither angel nor spirit, but the Pharisees hold to both, the resurrection and the world of spirits. 9The shouting grew loud, and some experts in the law from the Pharisees’ party got to their feet and fought the point: “We see no fault in this man. And if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, what then?” 10The dispute became so fierce that the tribune feared Paul would be pulled apart between them. He told the troops to go down, seize Paul out of the middle of them, and take him into the barracks.

Take courage

11The following night the Lord came and stood beside Paul. “Take courage,” he said. “Just as you have borne witness to me in Jerusalem, you must bear witness in Rome as well.”

More than forty men under a curse

12When day came, a group of Jews banded together and swore an oath, calling down a curse on themselves if they ate or drank anything before they had killed Paul. 13More than forty men took part in this plot. 14They went to the chief priests and the elders and told them, “We have put ourselves under a solemn curse: we will not taste a thing until we have killed Paul. 15So now you and the council must tell the tribune to bring Paul down to you, claiming that you want to look into his case more closely. We will be waiting to kill him before he ever reaches you.”

16But Paul’s nephew, the son of his sister, got word of the ambush. He made his way into the barracks and warned Paul. 17Paul called over one of the centurions and said, “Bring this young man to the tribune; he has news for him.” 18The centurion brought him to the tribune and reported, “The prisoner Paul called me over and asked me to take this young man to you, since he has a message for you.” 19The tribune took hold of his hand, led him off to one side by themselves, and asked him, “What is this news you have for me?” 20He answered, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as if the council meant to look more carefully into his case. 21Do not let them persuade you. More than forty of their men are lying in wait for him. They have sworn under a curse not to eat or drink until they have killed him, and they are ready now, only waiting for you to say yes.” 22The tribune sent the young man away with a warning: “Do not let anyone know you told me about this.”

Sent by night to Felix the governor

23Then he summoned two of his centurions and told them, “Have 200 soldiers ready to leave for Caesarea at nine o’clock tonight, with seventy horsemen and 200 spearmen.” 24He also had them provide mounts for Paul to ride, so that he would reach Felix the governor safely. 25And he wrote a letter that went like this: 26“Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent Governor Felix: greetings. 27The Jews had taken hold of this man and were on the verge of killing him. I came on the scene with the troops and pulled him out of their hands, having found out that he was a Roman citizen. 28Since I wanted to learn the grounds of their charges against him, I had him brought before their council. 29I found he was being accused over points of their own law, but with nothing that called for death or chains. 30Word reached me that a plot was being laid against him, so I am sending him to you straight away, and I have told his accusers to state their case against him in your presence.”

31The soldiers followed their instructions: they took charge of Paul and marched him through the night to Antipatris. 32The next day they left the horsemen to go on with him and went back to the barracks themselves. 33When the horsemen reached Caesarea, they handed the letter to the governor and brought Paul before him as well. 34After reading the letter, the governor asked what province Paul belonged to, and learned that it was Cilicia. 35“I will give you a full hearing,” he said, “once your accusers are here as well.” Then he gave orders for Paul to be held under guard in Herod’s praetorium.
fields.summary: Paul divides the council over the resurrection, and that night the Lord tells him to take courage. When more than forty men swear to kill Paul, the tribune sends him by night to Felix the governor in Caesarea.

fields.title: Acts 24
fields.body_html:
Tertullus brings the case against Paul

1Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some of the elders and a trained advocate named Tertullus, and they laid out their case against Paul before the governor. 2When Paul had been called in, Tertullus opened the prosecution: “Thanks to you we live in great peace, and your careful planning has set many things right for this nation. 3Most excellent Felix, we welcome all this in every way and in every place, with heartfelt thanks. 4But I do not want to keep you long, so I ask you, in your fairness, to give us a brief hearing. 5This man, we have found, is a public menace. He causes unrest among the Jews in every part of the world, and he is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. 6He even attempted to defile the temple, and we took hold of him. 8Question him yourself, and you will learn from him all about the things we accuse him of.” 9The Jews who had come added their voices, claiming that it was all so.

Paul makes his defense before Felix

10The governor signaled to Paul to speak, and he answered: “You have judged this nation for many years, and knowing that, I am glad to answer for myself before you. 11It is only twelve days, no more, since I went up to Jerusalem to worship, as you can find out. 12They never found me in the temple in debate with anyone or drawing a crowd together, nor in the synagogues, nor anywhere in the city. 13They have no proof to set before you for the things they now charge me with. 14This much I do acknowledge before you: it is as one who follows the Way, which they call a sect, that I serve the God of our ancestors. I believe all that accords with the law and all that stands written in the Prophets. 15My hope rests on God, and these men look for it too: that a resurrection is coming, of the righteous and the unrighteous alike. 16That is why I, for my part, take pains to live with a blameless conscience toward God and toward people at all times. 17I had been away for a number of years, and I came to bring charitable gifts to my people and to make offerings. 18I was doing this when they found me in the temple, ritually purified, with no crowd around me and no disorder. 19But some Jews from Asia were the ones who saw me. They should have come before you to accuse me, if they have any complaint against me. 20Otherwise, let the men who are here tell you what wrong they discovered in me when I stood before the council, 21unless it was the one sentence I called out as I stood among them: ‘I am being judged by you today over the resurrection of the dead.’”

22Felix knew a good deal about the Way, and he postponed the matter. He told them, “I will rule on your case once Lysias the tribune comes down.” 23He gave orders to the centurion: Paul was to stay in custody, but with some relief from strict confinement, and none of his own people were to be kept from helping him.

Felix and Drusilla hear Paul

24A few days afterward Felix arrived with Drusilla, his wife, a Jewish woman. He had Paul brought in and heard what he had to say about faith in Christ Jesus. 25As Paul reasoned with him about righteousness, self-control and the judgment that is coming, Felix became alarmed. “Leave me for now,” he answered. “I will call for you again when I find a suitable time.” 26At the same time he hoped for money from Paul, so he had him brought in quite often and talked with him.

27Two full years went by, and then Porcius Festus succeeded Felix. Felix wished to earn the favor of the Jews, so he left Paul behind in chains.
fields.summary: Tertullus brings the case against Paul before Felix, and Paul answers that he worships the God of his ancestors and hopes in the resurrection. Felix and Drusilla hear Paul speak about faith in Jesus, but Felix keeps Paul in custody for two years.

fields.title: Acts 25
fields.body_html:
Festus hears Paul, and Paul appeals to Caesar

1Festus had been in his province only three days when he left Caesarea and went up to Jerusalem. 2The chief priests and the most prominent Jews laid their charges against Paul before him and kept pressing him. 3They asked him for a favor that would harm Paul: to send for him to come to Jerusalem. They meant to lie in wait and kill him on the way. 4Festus replied that Paul was being held at Caesarea, and that he himself would soon be going back there. 5“So let your leading men travel down with me,” he said, “and if there is anything improper about this man, they can accuse him there.”

6He spent no more than eight or ten days with them and then went down to Caesarea. The day after he arrived, he took his place on the judgment seat and had Paul brought in. 7As soon as Paul appeared, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem crowded around him and laid many heavy charges on him, none of which they could prove. 8Paul’s defense was this: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar.” 9Festus, though, was looking to build up favor with the Jews. He turned to Paul and said, “Would you agree to go up to Jerusalem and have these matters judged there, with me presiding?” 10Paul said, “The court I stand before is Caesar’s, and here is where my case belongs. I have wronged the Jews in nothing, and you know this quite well yourself. 11If I am guilty and have done something for which I deserve to die, I do not ask to be spared death. But if there is nothing in what these men accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar!” 12Then Festus talked it over with his advisers and replied, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.”

Festus lays Paul’s case before King Agrippa

13After some days had gone by, King Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea on a visit of welcome to Festus. 14Their visit lasted many days, and during it Festus told the king about Paul. “Felix left a certain man behind in custody,” he said. 15“When I went to Jerusalem, the chief priests and the Jewish elders laid information against him and asked me to condemn him. 16I told them that it is not the Roman way to give anyone up as a favor until the accused person has met the accusers face to face and been given a chance to answer the charge. 17So when they had come here with me, I lost no time. The very next day I took my place on the judgment seat and had the man brought in. 18His accusers stood up, but the charges they brought were not the crimes I had been expecting. 19What they had against him were certain questions about their own religion, and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul asserted to be alive. 20I was unsure how to go about investigating questions like these, and so I asked whether he would like to go to Jerusalem and have the matter judged there. 21But Paul appealed to be held for the emperor’s decision, so I ordered him to be kept in custody until I can send him on to Caesar.” 22Agrippa told Festus, “I have been wanting to hear the man for myself.”

“You will hear him tomorrow,” Festus replied.

23So the following day Agrippa and Bernice came with a great show of splendor. They went into the hall of hearing along with the tribunes and the city’s most important men, and Festus gave the order for Paul to be brought. 24Then Festus spoke: “King Agrippa, and all of you who are here with us, look at this man. The entire Jewish people has come to me about him, in Jerusalem and here too, shouting that he has no right to go on living. 25I, for my part, saw that he had committed no crime that merits death. And as he has made an appeal to the emperor himself, I resolved to send him on. 26Yet I have nothing solid to put in a letter about him to my lord. That is why I have brought him out here before you all, King Agrippa, you above all, so that once he has been examined I may have something I can write. 27For to send a prisoner and not make clear what he is charged with seems senseless to me.”
fields.summary: Festus hears Paul’s case, and Paul appeals to Caesar. When King Agrippa and Bernice visit, Festus lays the case before them.

fields.title: Acts 26
fields.body_html:
Paul makes his defense before Agrippa

1Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak on your own behalf.” So Paul held out his hand and began to make his defense: 2“King Agrippa, I count myself fortunate that it is before you that I am to answer today for all the charges some Jews bring against me, 3especially as you know well all the customs and disputed questions of the Jews. So I ask you to hear me out with patience.

4All Jews know how I have lived from my youth, from the very start of my life among my own people and in Jerusalem. 5They have known me a long time, and if they were willing they could testify that I lived as a Pharisee, in the strictest sect of our religion. 6And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise God made to our ancestors. 7It is the promise our twelve tribes hope to see fulfilled as they worship God with devotion night and day. It is for this hope, Your Majesty, that I am accused by Jews. 8Why do any of you think it unbelievable that God raises the dead? 9I myself was once convinced that I had to do all I could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth, 10and that is what I did in Jerusalem. With authority from the chief priests I shut up many of God’s holy people in prison, and when they were condemned to die, I cast my vote against them. 11Again and again I had them punished in all the synagogues and tried to force them to blaspheme. My rage against them knew no bounds, and I hunted them down even in cities beyond our land.

A light from heaven on the road to Damascus

12That was my mission when I was on my way to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. 13At noon, Your Majesty, as I traveled along the road, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, blazing around me and the men traveling with me. 14We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice speaking to me in Hebrew: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It hurts you to kick against the goads.’ 15I asked, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ The Lord answered, ‘I am Jesus, the one you are persecuting. 16But rise, stand up on your feet. I have shown myself to you for a purpose: to choose you as my assistant and my witness, to tell what you have seen of me and what I will yet show you of me. 17I will keep you safe from your own people and from the Gentiles. I am sending you to them 18to open their eyes, so that they turn from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, and so receive forgiveness of their sins and a share in the inheritance among those sanctified by faith in me.’

19And so, King Agrippa, I did not resist the heavenly vision. 20I went first to the people of Damascus, then to Jerusalem and the whole country of Judea, and to the Gentiles too, and I told them all to repent and turn to God, and to live in a way that proves their repentance. 21It was for this that some Jews seized me in the temple and set about murdering me. 22God has helped me, and up to this very day I stand here bearing witness to people of low and high rank alike. I say only what the prophets and Moses foretold: 23that the Christ must suffer, and that, as the first to rise from the dead, he would announce light both to our own people and to the Gentiles.”

Festus interrupts, and Paul appeals to the king

24As Paul was saying this in his defense, Festus called out loudly, “You are out of your mind, Paul! All your great learning is pushing you into madness.” 25“I am not mad, most excellent Festus,” Paul replied. “The words I am speaking are truth and sound sense. 26The king understands these matters, and that is why I can speak to him so openly. I am sure that nothing of this has passed him by. After all, it did not happen in some out-of-the-way corner. 27King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe them.” 28Agrippa said to Paul, “In so short a time you are persuading me to become a Christian!” 29Paul answered, “Whether it takes little or much, my prayer to God is that not you alone but every one of my hearers today would come to be as I am, though without these chains.”

Nothing deserving death or chains

30Then the king stood up, with the governor, Bernice and those seated with them. 31After they had gone out, they said to each other, “Nothing this man does calls for death or prison.” 32Agrippa told Festus, “This man might have gone free, had he not appealed to Caesar.”
fields.summary: Paul makes his defense before Agrippa, telling of the light from heaven on the road to Damascus and his call to the Gentiles. Festus interrupts, Paul appeals to the king, and they agree that he has done nothing deserving death or chains.

fields.title: Acts 27
fields.body_html:
Paul sails for Italy

1Once our voyage to Italy had been decided, they placed Paul and a number of other prisoners in the custody of Julius, a centurion of the Augustan cohort. 2We went aboard a ship from Adramyttium that was due to call at ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us. 3The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius was considerate toward Paul and allowed him to go to his friends and be looked after by them. 4Putting out from there, we sailed on the sheltered side of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. 5We crossed the open water off Cilicia and Pamphylia and came to Myra in Lycia. 6At Myra the centurion came across an Alexandrian ship headed for Italy and transferred us to it. 7For many days we made slow headway and only with difficulty arrived off Cnidus. Since the wind would not let us hold our course, we sailed in the shelter of Crete, passing Salmone. 8Working our way along the shore with difficulty, we reached a place called Fair Havens, close to the town of Lasea.

9A great deal of time had gone by, and sailing was now hazardous, since even the Fast was past. So Paul gave them advice. 10“Men,” he said, “I can tell that this voyage is heading for harm and heavy loss, not only to the cargo and the ship but to our own lives too.” 11But the centurion put more trust in the helmsman and the owner of the ship than in what Paul was saying. 12The harbor was a poor place to spend the winter, so most of them were for putting out to sea again, in the hope of somehow getting to Phoenix to winter there. Phoenix is a harbor in Crete that faces both southwest and northwest.

The wind called Euraquilo

13When a light breeze came up from the south, they thought their plan could be carried out. So they raised anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore. 14But soon afterward a storm wind called Euraquilo, the northeaster, came rushing down off Crete. 15The ship was caught up in it and could not be turned into the wind, so we gave way and drifted before it. 16We ran in the lee of a small island called Cauda, and there, with great effort, we managed to secure the ship’s boat. 17After hoisting it aboard, the crew used ropes to brace the ship, passing them around the hull. They were afraid of being driven onto the sandbanks of the Syrtis, so they let down the sea anchor and were carried along in that way. 18The storm pounded us so fiercely that on the following day they started jettisoning the cargo. 19On the third day they took the ship’s spare gear and hurled it into the sea with their own hands. 20Day after day there was no sun and no stars to be seen, and the storm kept bearing down on us with great force. In the end every hope that we would come through alive was slipping away from us.

Take heart

21No one had eaten for a long time. Then Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have heeded me and stayed in Crete instead of setting out. You would have avoided all this damage and loss. 22Even so, I now urge you to take heart. Not one life among you will be lost; only the ship will go. 23For during this night an angel came and stood beside me, an angel of the God whose I am and whom I worship. 24He told me, ‘Paul, do not be afraid. You are to appear before Caesar. And look: God has granted you everyone who is on board with you.’ 25So take heart, men! I believe God: it will happen just the way I was told. 26But we have to be cast ashore on some island.”

27It was the fourteenth night, and we were drifting this way and that across the sea of Adria. Around midnight the crew started to suspect that land was coming near. 28They dropped a sounding line and found the water 120 feet deep. A little farther on they sounded again and found it 90 feet. 29They were afraid we might strike a rocky coast somewhere, so they threw out four anchors from the stern and prayed for morning to come. 30Meanwhile the sailors were trying to abandon the ship. They had lowered the boat into the sea on the excuse that they were about to run out anchors from the bow. 31But Paul told the centurion and the soldiers, “If these men do not stay on board, there is no way for you to be saved.” 32So the soldiers slashed the ropes of the boat and let it go.

Bread before daybreak

33While they waited for daybreak, Paul kept encouraging all of them to take some food. “This is the fourteenth day,” he said, “that you have kept watch without eating, taking nothing at all. 34So I urge you to take some food. It is for your own survival, since not a hair on the head of any of you will be lost.” 35When he had said this, Paul took bread and, with everyone watching, thanked God for it. Then he broke it and started eating. 36Everyone was cheered by this, and they too took some food. 37There were 276 of us on the ship in all. 38Once everyone had eaten enough, they threw the wheat overboard to lighten the ship.

All brought safely to land

39At daybreak the land was unfamiliar to them. But they caught sight of an inlet with a beach, and they made up their minds to drive the ship onto it if possible. 40They slipped the anchors and let them go into the sea, and at the same time they freed the lashings on the steering oars. Then they set the small front sail to catch the wind and steered toward the beach. 41But they came upon a place where two seas met and ran the vessel aground. Its bow dug in and held, unable to move, while the stern began to break apart under the violence of the waves. 42The soldiers meant to kill the prisoners, so that none of them could swim off and get away. 43The centurion, however, was determined to bring Paul through alive, and he held them back from what they meant to do. He told everyone who could swim to throw themselves into the sea first and head for the shore, 44and the rest to come after them, some on boards and others on wreckage from the ship. So it was that all of them came safely to land.
